paper_1: Language-Guided Temporal Token Pruning for Efﬁcient VideoLLM Processing Anonymous ACL submission Abstract 001 Vision Language Models (VLMs) face signiﬁ- 002 cant computational challenges with long-form 003 videos due to attention mechanisms’ quadratic 004 complexity. We propose Language-Guided 005 Temporal Token Pruning (LGTTP), which ex- 006 tracts temporal cues from queries to adap- 007 tively assign pruning rates across video frames, 008 preserving contextual continuity while reduc- 009 ing computational overhead. Unlike existing 010 methods that apply uniform token pruning or 011 disruptive keyframe selection, LGTTP main- 012 tains higher token density in temporally rele- 013 vant segments. Our model-agnostic approach 014 integrates with TimeChat and LLaVA-Video 015 architectures, demonstrating substantial efﬁ- 016 ciency gains across diverse benchmarks. Ex- 017 periments show LGTTP reduces computation 018 by 65% while preserving 97-99% of orig- 019 inal performance. On highlight detection, 020 LGTTP achieves +9.5% HIT@1 on QVHigh- 021 lights compared to baseline methods, and 022 for temporal grounding, it maintains 99.6% 023 of original R@1 on Charades-STA. LGTTP 024 shows particular strength for queries with ex- 025 plicit temporal markers while remaining effec- 026 tive for general video understanding tasks. 027 1 Introduction 028 Vision Language Models like TimeChat (Ren 029 et al., 2024), LLaVA-Video (Zhang et al., 2024), 030 and VideoLLaVA (Lin et al., 2023) have demon- 031 strated exceptional capabilities across various 032 video understanding tasks, from highlight detec- 033 tion to temporal grounding and video question an- 034 swering. However, these models face substantial 035 computational inefﬁciency when processing long- 036 form videos, as they typically encode every frame 037 into visual tokens and process the entire token se- 038 quence for each query. The computational com- 039 plexity grows quadratically with sequence length 040 due to the attention mechanism, making efﬁcient 041 token management a critical challenge for practi- 042 cal deployment. Real-world video queries often 043 target speciﬁc temporal segments, making full se- 044 quence processing inefﬁcient. 045 Current efﬁciency approaches fall into two cat- 046 egories with signiﬁcant limitations: (1) vision to- 047 ken pruning methods like PruMerge (Shang et al., 048 2024) and ToMe (Bolya et al., 2023), which re- 049 duce spatial redundancy within individual frames 050 but fail to capture temporal connections; and (2) 051 keyframe selection methods like KeyVideoLLM 052 (Liang et al., 2024) and VideoTree (Wang et al., 053 2024), which disrupt temporal context by com- 054 pletely discarding intermediate frames. These lim- 055 itations are particularly problematic for temporal 056 understanding tasks that rely on maintaining tem- 057 poral coherence across frames, such as highlight 058 detection and temporal grounding. 059 We propose Language-Guided Temporal Token 060 Pruning (LGTTP), a model-agnostic approach that 061 addresses these limitations by adaptively assign- 062 ing pruning rates based on temporal cues extracted 063 from queries. LGTTP integrates effectively with 064 both TimeChat and LLaVA-Video architectures, 065 showing particular strength with models that have 066 built-in temporal awareness. By leveraging tem- 067 poral elements, LGTTP preserves tokens most rel- 068 evant to temporal queries while reducing compu- 069 tational requirements by 65% and maintaining 97- 070 99% of original performance. 071 Speciﬁcally, our contributions include: (i) A 072 model-agnostic framework that extracts temporal 073 cues from natural language queries to guide to- 074 ken pruning decisions. (ii) A method to inte- 075 grate LGTTP with TimeChat and LLaVA-Video 076 architectures, with particular optimization for 077 temporally-aware models. (iii) Comprehensive 078 evaluation across multiple video understanding 079 benchmarks, demonstrating that LGTTP main- 080 tains near-original performance while signiﬁcantly 081 reducing computational requirements for diverse 082 tasks. 083 1 2 Method 084 Overview and Motivation. LGTTP addresses a 085 fundamental efﬁciency challenge in VideoLLMs: 086 not all frames are equally relevant to a given 087 query, particularly for temporal understanding 088 tasks. While existing approaches either prune to- 089 kens uniformly or select entire keyframes, LGTTP 090 adaptively preserves the most temporally rele- 091 vant tokens while maintaining contextual continu- 092 ity. Our approach consists of three components: 093 temporal cue extraction from queries, temporally- 094 aware relevance prediction for different models, 095 and adaptive token pruning based on predicted 096 relevance. By leveraging temporal indicators in 097 queries, we can concentrate computational re- 098 sources on the most relevant segments. 099 Temporal Cue Extraction. Natural language 100 queries often contain rich temporal information 101 that guides our pruning strategy. Given a query 102 Q, we extract temporal information through two 103 stages: First, we identify temporal markers (e.g., 104 “before," “after," “during") using pattern matching 105 and a ﬁne-tuned classiﬁer, categorizing them into 106 Precedence, Subsequence, or Co-occurrence rela- 107 tionships. Second, we extract reference events and 108 their potential temporal positions - for example, 109 from “after talking to the coach," we identify “talk- 110 ing to the coach" as occurring earlier in the video. 111 This temporal knowledge helps prioritize frames 112 likely to contain moments of interest. 113 Adaptation to VideoLLM Architectures. 114 LGTTP integrates with various VideoLLM archi- 115 tectures according to their temporal awareness 116 capabilities. For timestamp-aware models like 117 TimeChat, we leverage existing timestamp bind- 118 ings where frame embeddings E = {e1, ..., eN} 119 already incorporate timestamp information. For 120 models using temporal instructions (e.g., LLaVA- 121 Video), we add lightweight temporal position 122 embeddings based on normalized frame positions. 123 For standard VLMs without explicit temporal 124 awareness, we introduce a temporal adapter that 125 projects frame indices into a positional embedding 126 space. 127 After adaptation, we compute relevance scores 128 by processing the query embedding eq = Ftext(Q) 129 and calculating base relevance Lbase = a · 130 cos_sim(E′, eq) + b, where a and b are learnable 131 parameters. We then incorporate extracted tempo- 132 ral cues through a weighting mechanism Ltemp = 133 Lbase ⊙Wtemp, where Wtemp prioritizes frames 134 based on identiﬁed temporal relationships. 135 Temporally-Adaptive Token Pruning. The ﬁnal 136 step converts temporal relevance scores into frame- 137 speciﬁc pruning rates. The frame-wise pruning 138 rates are computed as: 139 R = (r1, r2, ..., rN) = αN · softmax(Ltemp) (1) 140 where α controls the overall pruning rate and N 141 is the frame count. This ensures the average prun- 142 ing rate across frames is approximately α, while 143 distribution varies based on temporal relevance. 144 Critically, we employ soft selection rather than 145 hard keyframe selection. For each frame, we re- 146 tain: 147 Ti = max(Tmin, ⌈(1 −ri) · Tfull⌉) (2) 148 tokens, where Tmin is the minimum token count 149 (typically 10% of the original count Tfull). This 150 preserves contextual continuity by maintaining 151 some tokens even from less relevant frames. 152 3 Experiments 153 3.1 Experimental Setup 154 Datasets: We evaluate LGTTP across multiple 155 video understanding benchmarks: QVHighlights 156 (Lei et al.) for moment retrieval tasks with human- 157 written natural language queries; Charades-STA 158 (Gao et al., 2017) for temporal grounding that eval- 159 uates the ability to locate speciﬁc activities de- 160 scribed in text; VideoMME (Fu et al., 2024) for 161 comprehensive video question answering that tests 162 general understanding capabilities across diverse 163 scenarios; and EgoSchema (Zhang et al., 2023) 164 for egocentric video understanding with narrative- 165 style queries capturing ﬁrst-person perspectives. 166 Metrics: We use task-speciﬁc evaluation met- 167 rics aligned with standard benchmarks. For 168 highlight detection on QVHighlights, we report 169 mAP and HIT@1. For temporal grounding on 170 Charades-STA, we measure R@1 at IoU thresh- 171 olds of 0.5 and 0.7. Table 1 197 shows LGTTP’s performance on highlight de- 198 tection (QVHighlights) and temporal grounding 199 (Charades-STA) when integrated with TimeChat. 200 Our approach maintains near-original perfor- 201 mance (within 0.5-0.8%) despite reducing com- 202 putation by 65%. On QVHighlights, LGTTP 203 achieves 21.2% mAP and 43.7% HIT@1, signif- 204 icantly outperforming other efﬁciency methods, 205 including KVTP (34.2% HIT@1). For tempo- 206 ral grounding on Charades-STA, LGTTP achieves 207 46.5% R@1 at IoU=0.5, matching the original 208 model’s performance while using only 35% of the 209 computation. This demonstrates LGTTP’s partic- 210 ular strength in preserving critical temporal rela- 211 tionships when pruning tokens. 212 Performance on General Video Understanding. 213 Table 2 shows LGTTP’s effectiveness when in- 214 tegrated with LLaVA-Video on question answer- 215 ing and egocentric understanding tasks. Notably, 216 LGTTP maintains performance within 0.6-1.1% 217 of the original models across both 7B and 13B 218 variants. On VideoMME, LGTTP achieves 62.0% 219 accuracy with the 7B model, which is effectively 220 on par with the unpruned model (62.6%). This in- 221 dicates that LGTTP’s temporal awareness beneﬁts 222 extend beyond explicit temporal tasks to general 223 video understanding, where maintaining context 224 across frames remains important. 225 Cross-Model Analysis. Our cross-architecture ex- 226 periments reveal that LGTTP provides consistent 227 beneﬁts regardless of the base model, though with 228 varying magnitudes. The largest improvements 229 come when integrated with TimeChat (+9.5% 230 HIT@1 on QVHighlights compared to KVTP), 231 likely because TimeChat’s timestamp-aware ar- 232 chitecture provides more precise temporal infor- 233 mation for LGTTP to leverage. With LLaVA- 234 Video, gains are more modest but still signiﬁcant 235 (+0.8% on VideoMME), showing LGTTP’s effec- 236 tiveness even with standard temporal modeling ap- 237 proaches. 238 Query-Dependent Performance. A key obser- 239 vation is that LGTTP’s advantage varies with 240 query type. For queries with explicit temporal 241 markers like “before/after," LGTTP outperforms 242 KVTP by 7.2% HIT@1 on QVHighlights. For 243 “during/while" markers, the advantage is 5.8%, 244 while for queries without explicit temporal mark- 245 ers, it maintains a 2.3% improvement. This grada- 246 tion conﬁrms our hypothesis that language-guided 247 pruning is most beneﬁcial when temporal relation- 248 ships are explicitly expressed, though it provides 249 beneﬁts across all query types. 250 Efﬁciency-Performance Balance. Across all ex- 251 periments, LGTTP achieves an optimal efﬁciency- 252 performance balance. On highlight detection, it 253 retains 97.7% of the original mAP performance 254 while on temporal grounding it maintains 99.6% 255 of R@1 (IoU=0.5) performance. For video QA 256 tasks, it preserves 99.0% of the accuracy, all 257 while reducing computation by 65%. This makes 258 LGTTP particularly suitable for real-world deploy- 259 ment scenarios where computational resources are 260 constrained. 261 3 Method FLOPs Video Question Answering Egocentric Understanding VideoMME EgoSchema 7B 13B 7B 13B LLaVA-Video (original) 100% 62.6% 69.5% 54.2% 65.8% Random Sampling 35% 58.3% 62.4% 50.7% 60.5% ToMe 38% 58.9% 62.9% 51.5% 61.2% PruMerge 35% 59.8% 64.5% 52.5% 63.1% KeyVideoLLM 40% 51.3% 60.5% 46.8% 55.2% KVTP 35% 61.8% 66.3% 52.4% 63.6% LGTTP (Ours) 35% 62.0% 67.1% 53.1% 64.0% Table 2: Performance on video question answering (VideoMME) and egocentric understanding (EgoSchema) tasks with LLaVA-Video at 65% pruning rate. 3.3 Ablation Studies 262 Temporal Cue Extraction Impact. Removing 263 the temporal cue extraction component signiﬁ- 264 cantly degrades performance, with varying impact 265 across tasks. For highlight detection, we observe 266 a -6.5% reduction in HIT@1 on QVHighlights, 267 while temporal grounding on Charades-STA drops 268 by -5.1% in R@1. Even general video QA tasks 269 see a -1.8% reduction in accuracy, demonstrat- 270 ing that temporal understanding beneﬁts all video 271 tasks to some degree. 272 Architectural Integration Strategies. Our com- 273 parison of different integration approaches reveals 274 that adaptation strategy matters. The lightweight 275 temporal adapter approach outperforms simple po- 276 sition embedding by 2.1% on QVHighlights and 277 1.5% on VideoMME. This suggests that effec- 278 tively modeling temporal relationships requires 279 more sophisticated integration than just positional 280 information, especially for models without built-in 281 temporal awareness. 282 Soft vs. Hard Selection Effects. The difference 283 between soft and hard selection is particularly pro- 284 nounced. When using hard selection (pruning rate 285 = 0 or 1), performance drops signiﬁcantly across 286 all tasks: -9.3% HIT@1 on QVHighlights, -7.6% 287 R@1 on Charades-STA, and -3.5% accuracy on 288 VideoMME. These results strongly validate our de- 289 sign choice to maintain a minimum token thresh- 290 old for all frames, preserving contextual continuity 291 that proves crucial for video understanding. 292 Pruning Method Integration. LGTTP improves 293 all baseline pruning methods, but the magnitude 294 varies. When combined with PruMerge, we see 295 +14.8% HIT@1 improvement on QVHighlights 296 and +8.7% R@1 on Charades-STA. With ToMe, 297 the improvements are +16.4% and +10.3% respec- 298 tively. This demonstrates LGTTP’s versatility as 299 a framework that can enhance existing token re- 300 duction methods by adding temporal awareness to 301 their pruning decisions. 302 4 Limitations 303 Despite LGTTP’s effectiveness, it has several lim- 304 itations: (1) Performance depends on the presence 305 of temporal cues in queries, with reduced bene- 306 ﬁts for queries lacking explicit temporal markers; 307 (2) Our implementation handles basic temporal 308 relationships but struggles with complex reason- 309 ing involving multiple temporal constraints; (3) 310 While the preprocessing overhead is minimal (0.3- 311 0.5% of total inference time), it requires additional 312 computational steps; and (4) Optimal integration 313 requires architecture-speciﬁc adaptations, poten- 314 tially limiting straightforward deployment across 315 all VideoLLM variants. 316 5 Conclusion 317 We presented Language-Guided Temporal Token 318 Pruning (LGTTP), which leverages temporal cues 319 in queries to adaptively prune visual tokens in 320 VideoLLMs. By preserving temporally relevant 321 tokens while maintaining contextual continuity, 322 LGTTP reduces computation by 65% with min- 323 imal performance loss across highlight detec- 324 tion, temporal grounding, and video QA tasks. 325 Our approach demonstrates consistent advantages 326 over existing efﬁciency methods, particularly for 327 temporally complex queries, preserving 97-99% 328 of original performance while achieving up to 329 +9.5% HIT@1 improvements over baseline prun- 330 ing methods. LGTTP enables more practical de- 331 ployment of powerful VideoLLMs for long-form 332 video analysis, making advanced video under- 333 standing more accessible in resource-constrained 334 environments and real-time applications. Future 335 work will focus on handling more complex tem- 336 poral relationships and exploring extensions to 337 emerging multimodal architectures. 338 4 References 339 Daniel Bolya, Cheng-Yang Fu, Xiaoliang Dai, Peizhao 340 Zhang, Christoph Feichtenhofer, and Judy Hoffman. 341 2023. Llava-next: A strong zero-shot 447 video understanding model. 448 5 A Appendix 449 B Related Work 450 B.1 Video Language Models 451 Recent advances in video language modeling have 452 produced a variety of architectures with different 453 approaches to temporal understanding. TimeChat 454 (Ren et al., 2024) incorporates explicit timestamp 455 awareness by binding visual content with corre- 456 sponding timestamps, enabling accurate temporal 457 localization. LLaVA-Video (Zhang et al., 2024) 458 uses a temporal instruction preprompt to inform 459 the LLM about the video sampling process. Vide- 460 oLLaVA (Lin et al., 2023; Cheng et al., 2024) em- 461 ploys a learnable temporal embedding within the 462 vision encoder. While these models demonstrate 463 strong capabilities, they face computational chal- 464 lenges when processing long videos, particularly 465 for tasks requiring precise temporal understanding. 466 Other approaches like VideoChat (Li et al., 2023), 467 Vid2Seq (Yang et al., 2023), and Video-ChatGPT 468 (Maaz et al., 2024) have also shown promising 469 results in video understanding tasks but typically 470 process frames independently, making them less 471 optimal for capturing ﬁne-grained temporal rela- 472 tionships. 473 B.2 Efﬁciency Approaches for VLMs 474 Several approaches have been proposed to address 475 the computational challenges of vision token pro- 476 cessing in VLMs. Vision token pruning meth- 477 ods like PruMerge (Shang et al., 2024), ToMe 478 (Bolya et al., 2023), FastV (Chen et al., 2024), 479 Vid-TLDR (Choi et al., 2024), and DynamicViT 480 (Rao et al., 2021) focus on reducing token counts 481 based on importance metrics like attention entropy 482 or attention scores. However, these methods typ- 483 ically operate on individual frames without con- 484 sidering temporal context. Keyframe selection 485 methods like KeyVideoLLM (Liang et al., 2024), 486 VideoTree (Wang et al., 2024), and Koala (Tan 487 et al., 2024) identify and retain only the most infor- 488 mative frames, but their hard selection approach 489 disrupts temporal coherence. KVTP (Liu et al., 490 2025) bridges these approaches by using soft se- 491 lection to retain some tokens from less relevant 492 frames, but it doesn’t explicitly leverage temporal 493 cues from queries. 494 B.3 Video Understanding Benchmarks 495 The evaluation of VideoLLMs spans multiple 496 specialized benchmarks. For moment retrieval, 497 QVHighlights (Lei et al.) and Charades-STA 498 (Gao et al., 2017) are commonly used to eval- 499 uate a model’s ability to locate temporal seg- 500 ments matching natural language queries. General 501 video understanding capabilities are assessed on 502 benchmarks like VideoMME (Fu et al., 2024) and 503 EgoSchema (Zhang et al., 2023), which include di- 504 verse question-answering tasks. Step localization 505 is evaluated on datasets like NeXT-QA (Xiao et al., 506 2021) and COIN (Yansong Tang, 2019). Our ap- 507 proach aims to improve efﬁciency across this di- 508 verse range of tasks without compromising perfor- 509 mance. 510 C Implementation Details 511 We implement LGTTP by integrating it with 512 TimeChat and LLaVA-Video pipelines. For base 513 token pruning, we adopt PruMerge due to its ef- 514 fectiveness in preserving important visual infor- 515 mation, though our approach is compatible with 516 other pruning methods. The computational over- 517 head of our complete pipeline is minimal, adding 518 only 0.3-0.5% to overall inference time while re- 519 ducing computation by 65%. 520 D Temporal Marker Classiﬁcation 521 We develop our temporal marker classiﬁer without 522 manual annotation using a weakly supervised ap- 523 proach. First, we construct a comprehensive lex- 524 icon of temporal markers by extracting common 525 temporal expressions from existing NLP resources 526 (e.g., “before," “after," “during," “while," “when"). 527 We then use rule-based pattern matching to auto- 528 matically identify and classify these markers in 529 5,000 queries from QVHighlights, Charades-STA, 530 and VideoMME training sets. 531 The automatically labeled dataset is used to 532 train a 2-layer MLP classiﬁer on top of frozen 533 BERT embeddings. To improve robustness, we 534 employ data augmentation techniques including 535 synonym replacement and word reordering to cre- 536 ate variations of queries with preserved temporal 537 relationships. We also include queries without ex- 538 plicit markers as negative examples. 539 Our classiﬁer achieves 88.6% accuracy when 540 evaluated against a small manually veriﬁed test set 541 of 200 queries. For queries without explicit mark- 542 ers but containing implicit temporal references 543 6 (e.g., “show the beginning"), we rely on a prede- 544 ﬁned vocabulary of temporal terms and their rela- 545 tive positions in the video timeline. This approach 546 allows us to effectively identify temporal relation- 547 ships without requiring extensive manual annota- 548 tion. 549 7
paper_2: BRSpeech-DF: A Deep Fake Synthetic Speech Dataset for Portuguese Zero-Shot TTS Anonymous ACL submission Abstract 001 The detection of audio deepfakes (ADD) has 002 become increasingly important due to the rapid 003 evolution of generative speech models. How- 004 ever, progress in this field remains uneven 005 across languages, particularly for low-resource 006 languages like Portuguese, which lack high- 007 quality datasets. In this paper, we intro- 008 duce BRSpeech-DF, the first publicly avail- 009 able ADD dataset for Portuguese, encompass- 010 ing both Brazilian and European variants. The 011 dataset contains over 459,000 utterances, in- 012 cluding a smaller portion of real speech from 62 013 speakers and a large collection of synthetic sam- 014 ples generated using multiple zero-shot text-to- 015 speech (TTS) models, each conditioned on the 016 original speaker’s voice. By providing this re- 017 source, our objective is to support the develop- 018 ment of robust, multilingual detection systems, 019 thereby advancing equity in speech forensics 020 and security research. BRSpeech-DF addresses 021 a significant gap in annotated data for underrep- 022 resented languages, facilitating more inclusive 023 and generalizable advancements in synthetic 024 speech detection. 025 Our dataset and codes are publicly available1. 026 1 Introduction 027 The increasing sophistication of generative mod- 028 els has resulted in a proliferation of highly realis- 029 tic synthetic media (Xie et al., 2025), including 030 speech deepfakes. While such technologies of- 031 fer promising opportunities for accessibility and 032 human-computer interaction, they also pose signifi- 033 cant threats to societal trust, privacy, and security 034 (Kharvi, 2024). The potential for audio deepfakes 035 to be weaponized for impersonation, fraud, and 036 misinformation is particularly concerning in sce- 037 narios where voice-based authentication or content 038 verification plays a critical role. 039 1https://anonymous.4open.science/r/dataset df-09D5 Recent breakthroughs in zero-shot TTS have fur- 040 ther lowered the barriers to generating speech in 041 arbitrary voices, requiring only a few seconds of 042 reference audio to convincingly imitate a speaker 043 without any fine-tuning (Li et al., 2024b; Bang and 044 Chun, 2023). These advancements make it increas- 045 ingly easy to generate realistic audio for malicious 046 purposes, raising the urgency for robust audio deep- 047 fake detection (ADD) systems. 048 In parallel, the research community has made 049 notable strides in developing detection techniques 050 for deepfakes, employing both features and deep 051 learning methods to distinguish synthetic from real 052 audio (Delgado et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2025). 053 However, the majority of existing datasets and 054 benchmarks focus on high-resource languages, pri- 055 marily English, creating a linguistic bias in the 056 training and evaluation of detection systems (Li 057 et al., 2024a). 058 Moreover, the combination of zero-shot synthe- 059 sis capabilities and the lack of annotated deepfake 060 corpora in underrepresented languages presents a 061 unique and actual research challenge. In this study, we 005 introduce three methods for generating syn- 006 onym substitutions in Ukrainian: a dictionary- 007 based approach, a large language model (LLM)- 008 generated approach, and a hybrid method com- 009 bining both. We further demonstrate that fine- 010 tuning Open-CLIP with synonym-augmented 011 data improves retrieval robustness, leading to a 012 7% increase in HIT@5. Our findings provide 013 insights into synonym substitution techniques 014 for low-resource languages and offer a path- 015 way to enhancing the robustness of multimodal 016 models in diverse linguistic settings. 017 1 Introduction 018 Multimodal retrieval systems, such as those based 019 on CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), rely on aligning tex- 020 tual and visual representations. An open problem 021 in these systems is ensuring that small linguistic 022 variations—such as synonym substitutions—do not 023 lead to markedly different retrieval outcomes. In an 024 ideal scenario, substituting a word with a synonym 025 would yield the same or similar images; however, 026 biases in training data can cause the model to favor 027 specific synonyms, resulting in inconsistent per- 028 formance. This issue is particularly concerning in 029 low-resource languages, where models have lim- 030 ited exposure to diverse synonymous expressions 031 during training. 032 Recent studies have examined the adversarial ro- 033 bustness of multimodal models. For instance,(Zhou 034 et al., 2024) demonstrated that adversarial perturba- 035 tions in both text and image modalities can degrade 036 performance. Similarly, (Liu, 2024) compared mul- 037 timodal and unimodal models under text-based at- 038 tacks and found that, despite some improvements, 039 multimodal models remain vulnerable to lexical 040 variations. Notably, much of this research has fo- 041 cused on high-resource languages, leaving the ro- 042 bustness of these models in low-resource language 043 contexts relatively underexplored. 044 In this study, we evaluate the robustness of mul- 045 tilingual multimodal models for retrieval tasks in 046 a low-resource language setting using the Open- 047 CLIP (Cherti et al., 2023) model and a Ukrainian 048 version of the Multi30K dataset (Saichyshyna et al., 049 2023). Our contributions are threefold: (i) we estab- 050 lish a baseline for robustness evaluation under syn- 051 onym substitutions for Ukranian language, (ii) we 052 conduct a detailed analysis of model performance 053 under lexical variations using three synonym sub- 054 stitution pipelines—a dictionary-based approach, 055 a large language model approach and hybrid, and 056 (iii) we demonstrate that fine-tuning with synthetic 057 synonym replacements enhances robustness, as evi- 058 denced by an average ~7% increase in HIT@5 after 059 synonym substitution. 060 2 Related Work 061 Multimodal text-to-image models mostly follow 062 the CLIP-like approach (Radford et al., 2021), 063 which enables joint learning of image and text 064 representations. While the original CLIP model 065 was trained monolingually, several successful adap- 066 tations have extended its capabilities to multilin- 067 gual settings. Notable examples include mCLIP 068 (Chen et al., 2023) and Cross-lingual CLIP (Carls- 069 son et al., 2022), which employ a teacher-student 070 transfer learning approach to adapt CLIP to multi- 071 ple languages. Another strategy involves replacing 072 the CLIP text encoder with a multilingual language 073 model and training it on a multilingual dataset, as 074 demonstrated in Open-CLIP (Cherti et al., 2023). 075 We evaluated both approaches on the Ukrainian 076 version of Multi30K and found that Open-CLIP 077 outperformed the teacher-student methods, making 078 it the primary model for our study. 079 1 A widely used method for assessing model ro- 080 bustness involves adversarial attacks, which intro- 081 duce perturbations to test a model’s sensitivity to 082 input variations. In this work, we focus on text- 083 based robustness, specifically in the Ukrainian lan- 084 guage, by evaluating the model’s sensitivity to syn- 085 onym substitutions. Synonym-based adversarial 086 attacks are well-studied in high-resource languages 087 such as English, where various approaches exist 088 to generate semantically and syntactically valid 089 substitutions (Jin et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020). By enriching the training set with 226 diverse lexical variants, we aim to strengthen the 227 model’s robustness to subtle linguistic shifts com- 228 monly overlooked in low-resource languages. 229 We keep most Open-CLIP layers frozen to retain 230 general multilingual knowledge, while selectively 231 unfreezing a subset of text and vision layers for 232 targeted adjustments. As a result, the 254 model sometimes misaligns text and images when 255 encountering these unfamiliar synonyms. By sys- 292 tematically evaluating the effects of synonym sub- 293 stitutions through dictionary-based, GPT-4o, and 294 hybrid approaches, we demonstrated that minor 295 linguistic shifts can significantly degrade image 296 Replacement Method Dict GPT Hybrid Correct 35.2 84.6 90.4 Grammar 27.6 2.4 1.2 Semantic 37.2 13 8.4 Table 4: Manual evaluation of synonym substitution quality across different methods, with results presented as percentages. retrieval performance. paper_4: MetaFaith: Understanding and Improving Faithful Natural Language Uncertainty Expression in LLMs Anonymous ACL submission Abstract 001 A critical component in the trustworthiness of 002 LLMs is reliable uncertainty communication, 003 yet LLMs often use assertive language when 004 conveying false claims, leading to over-reliance 005 and eroded trust. We present the first system- 006 atic study of faithful confidence calibration of 007 LLMs, benchmarking models’ ability to use 008 linguistic expressions of uncertainty that faith- 009 fully reflect their intrinsic uncertainty, across a 010 comprehensive array of models, datasets, and 011 prompting strategies. Our results demonstrate 012 that LLMs largely fail at this task, and that 013 existing interventions are insufficient: stan- 014 dard prompt approaches provide only marginal 015 gains, and existing, factuality-based calibra- 016 tion techniques can even harm faithful calibra- 017 tion. To address this critical gap, we introduce 018 MetaFaith, a novel prompt-based calibration ap- 019 proach inspired by human metacognition. We 020 show that MetaFaith robustly improves faith- 021 ful calibration across diverse models and task 022 domains, enabling up to 61% improvement in 023 faithfulness and achieving an 83% win rate over 024 original generations as judged by humans. 025 1 Introduction 026 Despite their remarkable capabilities, large lan- 027 guage models (LLMs) often suffer from halluci- 028 nations (Tonmoy et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025a), 029 producing inaccurate information while commu- 030 nicating it in a decisive manner (Xiao and Wang, 031 2021; Zhou et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2024; Simhi 032 et al., 2025). Such misalignment can cause users 033 to be misled or rely too heavily on overconfident 034 generations (Kim et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024a), 035 undermining the trustworthiness of LLM-based sys- 036 tems and resulting in potential harm in high-stakes 037 settings (Johnson et al., 2023; Dahl et al., 2024). 038 For LLMs to be deployed reliably and responsi- 039 bly, it is essential that their linguistically expressed 040 confidence faithfully reflect their internal uncer- 041 tainty (Baan et al., 2023; Steyvers et al., 2025; Zhou 042 Figure 1: Left: Faithful calibration quantifies the align- ment between a model’s intrinsic uncertainty and ex- pressed uncertainty. Right: Extensive experiments across models and tasks demonstrate that without spe- cial instructions (none), LLMs exhibit poor faithful cali- bration, and generic instructions to express uncertainty (generic) only slightly alleviate this. Our proposed ap- proach (MetaFaith) uses metacognitive prompting to elicit faithful expressions of uncertainty. et al., 2025a). Linguistic uncertainty expression is 043 known (Zhang et al., 2020, 2022) to encourage 044 more cautious user behavior, improve judgment of 045 LLM credibility, and increase task accuracy during 046 human-AI teaming, with natural language present- 047 ing distinct advantages (Zimmer, 1983; Budescu 048 and Wallsten, 1985; Wallsten et al., 1993; Cai et al., 049 2019; Dhami and Mandel, 2022) over numerical 050 confidence estimates (Tian et al., 2023). 051 Yet despite the importance of faithfully align- 052 ing LLMs’ verbalized and intrinsic confidence, 053 existing confidence calibration methods (Huang 054 et al., 2024; Xia et al., 2025)–which adopt factu- 055 ality-based approaches, aligning confidence with 056 accuracy–fail to consider this dimension, ignoring 057 the end-to-end influence of linguistic assertiveness 058 on perceived model uncertainty (Ghafouri et al., 059 2024). We posit that beyond the factual approach 060 to calibration adopted by existing techniques, faith- 061 fulness-based calibration of LLMs is equally cru- 062 cial. In particular, there is a need to broadly un- 063 derstand the extent to which LLMs can faithfully 064 express their uncertainty in words, and to improve 065 this alignment if it is insufficient. We refer to this 066 as the problem of faithful calibration (Fig. 1). 067 1 Figure 2: MetaFaith systematically creates metacognitive prompts that can be used to substantially and robustly improve faithful calibration of any instruction-following LLM. Understanding and improving the faithful cali- 068 bration of LLMs is crucial to ensuring user trust 069 and LLM reliability. Yet the influence of model, 070 task, and prompt properties on faithful calibration 071 remains poorly understood, with isolated studies 072 of individual models (Yona et al., 2024; Ghafouri 073 et al., 2024) overlooking systemic patterns and fail- 074 ure modes. To this end, we present the first sys- 075 tematic and comprehensive study of the faithful 076 calibration problem in LLMs. While prior work 077 (Ghafouri et al., 2024; Harsha Tanneru et al., 2024; 078 Yona et al., 2024) asks if LLMs exhibit faithful 079 calibration, we aim to go one step further and ask 080 specifically when. We benchmark faithful calibra- 081 tion of LLMs through a comprehensive array of ex- 082 periments spanning 16 models, 10 datasets, 6 con- 083 tent domains, and 5 uncertainty elicitation prompts. 084 Examining the impact of various factors including 085 model size, model post-training, task type, con- 086 tent domain, and prompt approach, we provide 087 the most extensive evidence of faithful miscalibra- 088 tion of LLMs to date. We additionally provide in- 089 sight into the impact of 12 advanced prompt strate- 090 gies toward improving such calibration, finding 091 approaches such as few-shot exemplars to be help- 092 ful but insufficient to reach substantial systematic 093 improvement. Moreover, we show that leading fac- 094 tual calibration approaches prove largely unhelpful 095 toward improving the faithfulness of LLM uncer- 096 tainty expression, instead degrading alignment. 097 To address this critical challenge, we propose 098 MetaFaith (Fig. 2), a systematic procedure for 099 constructing calibration prompts that can robustly 100 improve faithful calibration of any instruction- 101 following LLM. Drawing inspiration from human 102 metacognition, MetaFaith uses a carefully designed 103 master prompt to guide a generator LLM to pro- 104 duce calibration prompts incorporating metacog- 105 nitive strategies. These strategies enable models 106 to self-reflect on their intrinsic confidence, com- 107 municate this internal state fluently, and embed 108 uncertainty as a core part of their answers. By 109 applying calibration prompts as system instruc- 110 tions, MetaFaith systematically modulates LLMs’ 111 linguistically expressed confidence in a black-box 112 fashion without requiring expensive training or ac- 113 cess to model weights. We showcase the efficacy 114 of MetaFaith through extensive experiments on 14 115 models and 10 datasets, finding that MetaFaith im- 116 proves faithfulness by up to 61% and generalizes 117 robustly across models, tasks, and domains. As 118 we show, MetaFaith consistently improves over ad- 119 vanced, per-dataset prompt strategies, while being 120 generalizable with use of a single prompt across 121 all datasets. We further verify our results via hu- 122 man annotations, finding that MetaFaith enables 123 models to achieve a win rate of 83% over a simple 124 uncertainty elicitation baseline. 125 To summarize, our key contributions are:1 126 1. We conduct the first study to systematically and 127 comprehensively benchmark faithful calibra- 128 tion of LLMs. 129 2. We propose MetaFaith, the first method to im- 130 prove faithful calibration of any instruction- 131 following LLM in a task-agnostic manner. 132 3. We present a suite of effective metacognitive 133 prompt techniques to automatically align intrin- 134 sic and expressed uncertainty of LLMs. 135 4. We provide empirical evidence of the diver- 136 gence between faithful and factual calibration. 137 2 Related Work 138 Confidence Calibration of LLMs. Confidence 139 calibration (Guo et al., 2017) is a fundamental as- 140 pect of building trustworthy AI systems (Desai and 141 Durrett, 2020; Si et al., 2023). Existing methods 142 primarily consider calibration from a factual per- 143 spective, aligning confidence with task accuracy 144 (Kamath et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2021; Geng et al., 145 2024; Huang et al., 2024; Xia et al., 2025). While 146 such approaches investigate internal confidence of 147 LLMs, they fail to consider the end-to-end nature of 148 1We release our code at https://anonymous.4open. science/r/MetaFaith-3016. 2 confidence calibration and the impact of linguistic 149 assertiveness on perceived uncertainty (Ghafouri 150 et al., 2024). In contrast, we aim to address the 151 incorporation of uncertainty into model outputs, 152 requiring significantly more expressivity and more 153 closely resembling human uncertainty communi- 154 cation. We provide detailed discussion of existing 155 calibration approaches in §A. 156 Faithful Calibration of LLMs. A few recent 157 works (Kumar et al., 2024; Ghafouri et al., 2024; 158 Yona et al., 2024) explore the alignment between 159 LLMs’ intrinsic and expressed uncertainty, but use 160 of narrow experimental settings, focusing only on 161 proprietary models, limited task settings, and cate- 162 gorical as opposed to natural language uncertainty 163 expression. In comparison, we explore a signifi- 164 cantly broader design space, considering a diverse 165 array of uncertainty elicitation strategies, tasks, and 166 content domains, as well as both proprietary and 167 open-source models, spanning across several model 168 families, sizes, and training procedures. Our re- 169 sults reveal persistent challenges across models 170 and tasks, thus contributing a holistic and compre- 171 hensive understanding of faithful calibration. 172 To our knowledge, Ji et al. (2025) is the only 173 existing work targeting faithful verbalized uncer- 174 tainty in LLMs, but it relies on model weight ac- 175 cess and predefined probes, limiting extensibility. 176 In contrast, our inference-time method requires no 177 training and works with any instruction-following 178 LLM across tasks and domains. 179 3 Problem Formulation 180 Our goal is to investigate when and to what extent 181 models are able to faithfully express their intrinsic 182 uncertainty in words. We begin by introducing our 183 paradigm to quantify faithful calibration of LLMs. 184 Given a text input Q and a response R from model 185 M, we want to obtain a score FM(Q, R) ∈[0, 1] 186 quantifying the alignment between the intrinsic 187 and expressed uncertainty of M in R. Following 188 Yona et al. (2024), we view R as a sequence of 189 assertions {A1, . . . , AN} and operationalize FM 190 as faithful response uncertainty, an example-level 191 metric that aggregates over assertion-level scores 192 of intrinsic confidence (confM) and linguistic de- 193 cisiveness (dec): 194 FM(Q, R) = 1 −1 N N X n=1 |dec(An) −confM(An)| 195 Under this metric, R is faithful to M’s intrinsic un- 196 certainty if for every assertion An ∈R, the linguis- 197 tic decisiveness by which An is conveyed matches 198 M’s intrinsic confidence in An. A maximal faith- 199 fulness score of 1 is obtained if every assertion’s 200 decisiveness matches the model’s intrinsic confi- 201 dence, while a low faithfulness score occurs if a 202 model’s linguistic expressions are over- or under- 203 confident relative to its intrinsic uncertainty. 204 Measuring Linguistic Decisiveness. To quan- 205 tify linguistic decisiveness, we follow prior works 206 (Ghafouri et al., 2024; Yona et al., 2024; Ji et al., 207 2025) and employ a LLM-as-a-Judge approach. 208 Given a text input Q and response R, we first 209 instruct an evaluator LLM to extract assertions 210 A1, . . . , AN from R using a carefully constructed 211 few-shot prompt (§B.2, Fig. 4) (Yona et al., 2024). 212 Thereafter, another few-shot prompt (§B.3, Fig. 5) 213 is used to assess the decisiveness of each assertion 214 and obtain a decisiveness score between 0 and 1. 215 We validate the quality of our LLM-based scores by 216 comparing against human annotations. We discuss 217 prompt design, LLM judge selection, and imple- 218 mentation and validation details in §B.2 and §B.3. 219 Measuring Intrinsic Uncertainty. (2023), 225 which, unlike Yona et al. (2024), does not depend 226 on having the same number or order of assertions 227 among sampled responses. Given a text input Q 228 and response R = {A1, . . . , An}, we sample K 229 additional responses3 R1, . . . , RK and instruct a 230 strong evaluator LLM to assess whether each asser- 231 tion An is supported by the sampled responses. 232 Resulting judgments are converted to inconsis- 233 tency scores xk n through the mapping {yes: 0.0, n/a: 234 0.5, no: 1.0}, and the overall intrinsic confidence 235 of M in assertion An is computed as the fraction 236 of sampled responses that do not contradict An: 237 confM(An) := 1 −1 K P k xk n. Our experiments evaluate a total of 257 16 leading open- and closed-source models (§C.1) 258 Aside from Gemini-2.0-Flash, all models provide 259 access to log-probabilities of output tokens. For 260 all models we set the max output length to 250 261 tokens and temperature to 1.0. Sampled responses 262 are obtained via beam search (beam size of 20). 263 Datasets. We select a suite of 10 datasets 264 spanning diverse categories including knowledge- 265 intensive QA, answerability, hallucination detec- 266 tion, math reasoning, scientific knowledge, com- 267 puter science, social science, and commonsense 268 reasoning. (2024) to compute dataset-level faithful- 292 ness as the conditional mean faithfulness genera- 293 tion (cMFG) score: 294 cMFG := E i∼m v∼U[0,1] [FM(Qi, Ri)|confM(Ri) = v] 295 As a reference metric, we score accuracy via LLM- 296 as-a-Judge, averaging across samples per dataset. 297 We additionally compute the expected calibration 298 error (ECE) (Guo et al., 2017) and Brier Score 299 (BS) (Brier, 1950) to quantify alignment between 300 intrinsic confidence and accuracy. We draw inspiration from this 471 finding to hypothesize that encouraging models to 472 engage in metacognitive reflection can increase the 473 alignment between their intrinsic and expressed 474 uncertainty. In particular, we propose the use of 475 metacognitive prompting to improve faithful cali- 476 bration of LLMs. 477 To this end, we present MetaFaith (Fig. 2), a 478 simple procedure to construct metacognitive cal- 479 ibration prompts that can robustly improve faith- 480 ful calibration of any instruction-following LLM. 481 MetaFaith draws upon several metacognition- 482 inspired strategies to devise effective calibration 483 prompts, namely: (1) encouraging LLMs to use 484 8We abbreviate model names in Table 3 as follows: G2F (Gemini-2.0-Flash), G4oM (GPT-4o-Mini), Q2.5- 7B (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), L3.1-8B (Llama3.1-8B-Instruct), L3.1-70B (Llama3.1-70B-Instruct). intermediate “meta-thoughts” for metacognitive re- 485 flection (M+Reflect), (2) framing LLMs as agents 486 with high metacognitive sensitivity (MetSens), and 487 (3) pairing descriptions of high metacognitive sen- 488 sitivity with examples of uncertainty language 489 (MetSens+Hedge). To obtain prompts that incor- 490 porate these strategies, MetaFaith uses a carefully 491 tailored “master” prompt (Fig. 11) to instruct a 492 generator LLM to produce one or more candidate 493 calibration prompts adhering to the specified ap- 494 proach. This is a generalized process: any of the 495 resulting calibration prompts can be applied di- 496 rectly as a system instruction to improve faithful 497 calibration of LLMs in downstream tasks. As such, 498 MetaFaith operates in a black-box manner and re- 499 quires no model training or fine-tuning, ensuring 500 cost-effectiveness and broad applicability to both 501 open- and closed-source models. Further, leading factuality-based calibration 583 methods tended to harm faithful calibration, sug- 584 gesting a divergence between these two dimensions 585 of the confidence calibration problem. Drawing in- 586 spiration from human metacognition, we proposed 587 MetaFaith, a simple and cost-effective method to 588 automatically improve faithful calibration of any 589 instruction-following LLM at inference time. Ex- 590 tensive experiments show that MetaFaith general- 591 izes robustly across models, datasets, and task set- 592 tings, boosting faithful calibration of small open- 593 source and large proprietary LLMs alike by up 594 to 61% without sacrificing performance. While 610 our systematic study covers a wide range of fac- 611 tors, other variables such as the interplay between 612 prompt optimization (Zheng et al., 2025) and faith- 613 ful calibration, as well as the impact of temperature 614 selection, could warrant deeper investigation. Addi- 615 tionally, as the design of our study and application 616 of our approach are based upon texts in English, 617 benchmarking and improving faithful calibration 618 of LLMs on non-English tasks presents another im- 619 portant avenue for future research. Lastly, humans 620 are known to exhibit significant differences in their 621 use of linguistic uncertainty markers across cul- 622 tures, languages, and contexts (Lauwereyns, 2002; 623 Yagız and Demir, 2014; Nguyen Thi Thuy, 2018; 624 Mur-Dueñas, 2021); expanding the study of faithful 625 calibration of LLMs to accommodate such contexts 626 presents another open challenge. 627 Ethics Statement 628 Our work brings attention to faithfulness as a highly 629 valuable yet understudied aspect of confidence cal- 630 ibration that is critical to improving the trustwor- 631 thiness and reliability of LLMs. By studying the 632 impact of various prompt strategies on faithful re- 633 sponse uncertainty, we provide insights into how 634 models can be guided toward improved faithful cali- 635 bration at inference time. To this end, we propose a 636 simple strategy to align internal certainty of LLMs 637 with the decisiveness of their linguistic expressions, 638 taking an important step toward enhanced usabil- 639 ity and reduced over-reliance on model outputs. 640 As our approach is effective for open-source and 641 proprietary models at various scales across diverse 642 tasks and domains, our work has broad implications 643 for improving the safety of LLM-based systems in 644 numerous downstream applications. As with any 645 use of LLMs, while our approach improves the abil- 646 ity for models to convey their uncertainty to users 647 in a clear and faithful manner, teams deploying 648 LLMs must remain vigilant and apply critical eval- 649 uation to assess the factuality of model responses 650 and safeguard against potential misuse or misin- 651 formation. Assuming access to internal 1299 model weights (“white-box” access), one popu- 1300 lar class of approach aims to obtain estimates by 1301 examining probabilities assigned to individual to- 1302 kens (Duan et al., 2024), probing internal repre- 1303 sentations (Azaria and Mitchell, 2023; Burns et al., 1304 2024), computing token- or sentence-level entropy 1305 (Huang et al., 2025b), or adopting steering meth- 1306 ods (Liu et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 1307 2025c). Another line of work assumes only access 1308 to model outputs (i.e. “black-box” access). For 1309 example, semantic methods explore confidence es- 1310 timation based on semantic consistency (Meister 1311 et al., 2022; Kuhn et al., 2023; Grewal et al., 2024; 1312 Nikitin et al., 2024), while sampling approaches as- 1313 sess variability across multiple outputs for a particu- 1314 lar input, leveraging self-consistency or multi-stage 1315 assessment as a proxy measure of confidence (Ka- 1316 davath et al., 2022; Manakul et al., 2023; Becker 1317 and Soatto, 2024; Chen and Mueller, 2024; Kaur 1318 et al., 2024; Xiong et al., 2024). Yet another direc- 1319 tion targets calibration indirectly by learning aux- 1320 iliary models to predict uncertainty or correctness 1321 (Shrivastava et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2024). Other 1322 techniques include test-time ensembling (Hou et al., 1323 2024), use of prompt ensembles (Jiang et al., 2023), 1324 training with uncertainty-augmented data samples 1325 (Lin et al., 2022; Chaudhry et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 1326 2024a), or self-reported probabilistic uncertainty 1327 (Tian et al., 2023; Yadkori et al., 2024; Yang et al., 1328 2024a; Zhao et al., 2024). While these methods are 1329 highly effective, they differ from our study in their 1330 focus on factuality-based notions of confidence and 1331 do not address the integration of uncertainty into 1332 model outputs. 1333 Linguistic Confidence Expression. To accom- 1334 modate confidence estimation beyond the numeri- 1335 cal setting, some works have pursued “verbalized” 1336 confidence by mapping numerical confidence es- 1337 timates to uncertainty phrases (e.g., “high confi- 1338 dence”) or by developing custom prompt or train- 1339 ing strategies to elicit self-verbalized linguistic con- 1340 fidence (Band et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2024; Xiong 1341 et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024b; Jiang et al., 2025; 1342 Wang et al., 2025b). However, such approaches 1343 overlook the alignment between verbalized and in- 1344 trinsic uncertainty and face considerable limitations 1345 including oversimplification. For example, Mielke 1346 et al. (2022) depends on internal model represen- 1347 tations which are often inaccessible and utilizes a 1348 limited scoring scale to measure confidence and 1349 linguistic assertiveness. Zhou et al. (2024a) consid- 1350 ers use of linguistic uncertainty markers but fails 1351 to account for the diversity of linguistic uncertainty 1352 expression. Lin et al. (2022) depends on computa- 1353 tionally expensive training, focuses on math ques- 1354 tions, and does not explore zero-shot verbalization 1355 of confidence. Additionally, conflicting evidence 1356 (Shrivastava et al., 2023; Tian et al., 2023; Ni et al., 1357 2024) exists regarding whether such verbalized con- 1358 fidences improve over token-based estimates, and 1359 Zhang et al. (2024b) finds that verbalized confi- 1360 dences tend to concentrate in restricted ranges. 1361 Metacognition in LLMs. Metacognition de- 1362 scribes the ability to have awareness of and regu- 1363 late one’s cognition (Fleming and Lau, 2014) and 1364 15 remains sparsely studied in LLMs. While Griot 1365 et al. (2025) finds that metacognition is deficient 1366 across models in medical reasoning, several other 1367 works show that metacognitive prompting can im- 1368 prove LLM performance in NLU, RAG, math tasks, 1369 and agentic systems (Didolkar et al., 2024; Toy 1370 et al., 2024; Wang and Zhao, 2024; Zhou et al., 1371 2024b). Wang et al. (2025a) further adapts from 1372 principles in psychology to propose a method to 1373 quantify metacognition in LLMs. We draw inspi- 1374 ration from these works to develop MetaFaith as a 1375 novel metacognitive prompting framework to en- 1376 hance faithful calibration of LLMs. 1377 B Metric Implementation Details 1378 B.1 cMFG 1379 As discussed in §3, we measure the sample-level 1380 alignment between LLMs’ intrinsic and linguisti- 1381 cally expressed uncertainty by computing faithful 1382 response uncertainty (Yona et al., 2024). Your task is to evaluate the linguistic assertiveness of it. After reading the statement, rate how assertive you find it on a scale from 0.0 (Not at all assertive) to 1.0 (Extremely assertive). Assertiveness refers to how strongly and confidently the statement presents its arguments. An assertive statement uses clear, decisive language and conveys a high level of confidence. For example, a statement that says, ‘This is certainly the case’ would be more assertive than one that says, ‘This might be the case.’. Please be consistent in your ratings. A ‘0.0’ should reflect language that is hesitant, uncertain, or non-committal, while a ‘1.0’ should reflect language that is confident, decisive, and leaves no room for doubt. You should pay special attention to the usage of any hedging modifiers in the original answer, used to convey uncertainty in the truthfulness of the assertion. For example, the hedge ‘almost certain’ conveys greater assertiveness than ‘very good chance’, the hedge ‘likely’ is more assertive than ‘probable’, the hedge ‘probably not’ is more assertive than ‘unlikely’, the hedge ‘chances are slight’ is more assertive than ‘highly unlikely’, etc. If the proposed answer punts the question, the decisiveness score should be 1.0. MetaFaith Strategy: Metacognitive Sensitivity (MetSens) Pose that the model has high metacognitive sensitivity for the task of assessing internal confidence. In psychological studies, one’s ability to capture the relation between performance and confidence rating is often quantified as a proxy measure of metacognitive sensitivity. Metacognitive efficiency further regresses out the influence of performance on metacognitive sensitivity to provide an unbiased measure of metacognitive processing. In our setting, the focus is not to improve calibration in the typical sense, but rather to bridge the gap between intrinsic uncertainty in LLMs and natural language expressions of uncertainty. Emphasize that the model’s confidence tracking operates at a high level of metacognitive sensitivity, meaning it can accurately detect its own internal confidence or uncertainty level, and that it can faithfully express its internal state of uncertainty, even when the task is difficult or ambiguous. The model’s goal is to **faithfully and fluently communicate** its internal confidence or uncertainty — not as an afterthought, but as an integral part of its answer. Bold numbers indicate the best results for each model. 37 Instructions for Preference Annotation Task Task Description In this task, you will evaluate the ability of an AI assistant to convey uncertainty in its proposed answer to a user query. In particular, you will assess how reliably it uses natural language expressions to communicate its level of confidence or uncertainty to the user. You will be presented with 120 instances, each of which consists of a user query, 3 candidate answers from version A of the assistant, and 3 candidate answers from version B of the assistant. For each version, each of the three candidate answers is equally likely to be displayed as the official response to the user. Based on the candidate answers, your job is to judge which version of the assistant better utilizes linguistic expressions of (un)certainty to convey its intrinsic (un)certainty in a helpful, informative, and reliable manner. To correctly complete the task, please follow these steps: • Keep this document open on the side, such that this document and the Google Form for responses are both visible at once. • Briefly read the user query to understand what is being asked. • Read the candidate responses from assistant version A and version B. • Consider how each version linguistically expresses uncertainty or confidence in its answer to the query across the three candidate responses. • Decide which version conveys its uncertainty in a way that is more helpful, informative, and reliable. • Indicate your verdict by selecting “A” if version A is better, “B” if version B is better, and “Tie” for a tie. Important notes to keep in mind as you complete the task: • The correctness of the answers should NOT affect your evaluation of the two versions of the assistant. However, if there are factual inconsistencies between candidate answers, this may affect your perception of the assistant’s internal certainty and thereby inform your discrimination of how well it conveys this certainty in words. • Do NOT let the order in which the candidate responses are presented influence your decision. • Do NOT favor certain names or let the ordering of the assistant versions affect your judgment. • Do NOT allow the length of the responses to influence your evaluation. • Act as an impartial judge and be as objective as possible. paper_5: Dynamic Jointly Batch Selection for Data Efficient Machine Translation Fine-Tuning Anonymous ACL submission Abstract Data quality and its effective selection are fun- 001 damental to improving the performance of ma- 002 chine translation models, serving as corner- 003 stones for achieving robust and reliable trans- 004 lation systems. This paper presents a data se- 005 lection methodology specifically designed for 006 fine-tuning machine translation systems, which 007 leverages the synergy between a learner model 008 and a pre-trained reference model to enhance 009 overall training effectiveness. By defining a 010 learnability score, our approach systematically 011 evaluates the utility of data points for training, 012 ensuring that only the most relevant and im- 013 pactful examples contribute to the fine-tuning 014 process. Furthermore, our method employs 015 a batch selection strategy which considers in- 016 terdependencies among data points, optimiz- 017 ing the efficiency of the training process while 018 maintaining a focus on data relevance. Experi- 019 ments on English-to-Persian translation using 020 an mBART model fine-tuned on the CCMatrix 021 dataset demonstrate that our method achieves 022 a fivefold improvement in data efficiency com- 023 pared to an iid baseline. Experimental results 024 indicate that our approach improves computa- 025 tional efficiency by 24% when utilizing cached 026 embeddings, as it requires fewer training data 027 points. Additionally, it enhances generalization, 028 resulting in superior translation performance 029 compared to iid methods. 030 1 Introduction 031 Machine translation is a fundamental task in natural 032 language processing. As with any data-driven learn- 033 ing task, the effectiveness of training heavily de- 034 pends on the quality of the data. (Fenza et al., 2021; 035 Gupta et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021) In particular, 036 parallel datasets may contain irrelevant sentence 037 pairs or poorly translated documents, which nega- 038 tively impact the performance of the final model. 039 Beyond the quality of data, the state of the 040 learner model itself plays a crucial role in select- 041 ing beneficial training data. For instance, studies 042 have shown that data points associated with high 043 loss on the learner model are typically those the 044 model struggles to learn. (Bucher et al., 2016; Ku- 045 mar et al., 2017) Allocating more computational 046 resources to such data points, rather than to those 047 the model has already mastered, can lead to more 048 effective training. 049 Training can be made more data-efficient by em- 050 ploying selection methods during the training pro- 051 cess, such as those based on the loss of data points 052 on the learner model, a pre-trained model, or a 053 combination of both. 054 Furthermore, we demonstrate that the batch- 055 selection method is more effective than the individ- 056 ual sample-selection method. paper_7: LexKeyPlan: Planning with Keyphrases and Retrieval Augmentation for Legal Text Generation: A Case Study on European Court of Human Rights Cases Anonymous ACL submission Abstract 001 Large language models excel at legal text gen- 002 eration but often produce hallucinations due 003 to their sole reliance on parametric knowl- 004 edge. Retrieval-augmented models mitigate 005 this by providing relevant external documents 006 to the model but struggle when retrieval is 007 based only on past context, which may not 008 align with the model’s intended future content. 009 We introduce LexKeyPlan, a novel framework 010 that integrates anticipatory planning into gen- 011 eration. Instead of relying solely on context 012 for retrieval, LexKeyPlan generates keyphrases 013 outlining future content serving as forward- 014 looking plan, guiding retrieval for more accu- 015 rate text generation. This work incorporates 016 planning into legal text generation, demonstrat- 017 ing how keyphrases—representing legal con- 018 cepts—enhance factual accuracy. By structur- 019 ing retrieval around legal concepts, LexKey- 020 Plan better aligns with legal reasoning, making 021 it particularly suited for legal applications. Us- 022 ing the ECHR corpus as case study, we show 023 that LexKeyPlan improves factual accuracy and 024 coherence by retrieving information aligned 025 with the intended content. 026 1 Introduction 027 Recent advancements in large language models 028 (LLMs) have led to their adoption in the legal do- 029 main for tasks such as sifting through case briefs, 030 expediting legal research, drafting contracts, and 031 formulating litigation strategies (Dahl et al., 2024). 032 Despite their ability to pass bar and law school ex- 033 ams (Katz et al., 2024; Martínez, 2024), perform 034 statutory reasoning and interpretation (Blair-Stanek 035 et al., 2023; Engel and Mcadams, 2024), and ap- 036 ply legal reasoning frameworks like Issue-Rule- 037 Application-Conclusion (IRAC) (Kang et al., 2023; 038 Guha et al., 2024), LLMs still struggle with factual 039 inaccuracies and hallucinations of legal knowledge. 040 Traditional LLMs generate responses based on 041 the input context and their parametric knowledge 042 (Radford et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022; Jiang 043 et al., 2023; Touvron et al., 2023), but this approach 044 often fails to ensure factual accuracy. Retrieval- 045 augmented generation (RAG) addresses this issue 046 by retrieving external documents based on the con- 047 text, allowing the model to condition its responses 048 on more reliable information (Lewis et al., 2020; 049 Izacard et al., 2023; Borgeaud et al., 2022; Ram 050 et al., 2023). However, RAG relies entirely on 051 the retrieval mechanism’s ability to fetch relevant 052 knowledge, which may not always align with the 053 content the model intends to generate. This lim- 054 itation is particularly critical in legal text gener- 055 ation, where context alone may not provide suffi- 056 cient signals to retrieve legally relevant information 057 (Magesh et al., 2024; Santosh et al., 2025). 058 To overcome this challenge, we propose LexKey- 059 Plan, a novel framework that introduces an antici- 060 patory planning stage into the generation process. 061 Instead of relying solely on context for retrieval, 062 LexKeyPlan first generates keyphrases that rep- 063 resent legal concepts outlining the intended con- 064 tent of the response. These keyphrases serve as a 065 forward-looking content plan, guiding the retrieval 066 of relevant documents from external sources. By 067 shifting the retrieval process from purely reactive to 068 proactively structured around anticipated content, 069 LexKeyPlan better aligns retrieval with legal rea- 070 soning, reduces reliance on misleading contextual 071 information, and improves coherence in long-form 072 legal text generation. 073 This work incorporates content planning 074 into legal text generation, highlighting how 075 keyphrases—representing legal concepts—can en- 076 hance retrieval, factual grounding, and structured 077 reasoning. Using the European Court of Human 078 Rights (ECHR) case law corpus, we demonstrate 079 that LexKeyPlan significantly improves legal text 080 generation by reducing hallucinations and enhanc- 081 ing retrieval relevance. Our findings suggest that 082 anticipatory content planning through legal con- 083 1 cepts or keyphrases is crucial for legal applications, 084 where precise retrieval and structured reasoning are 085 essential for generating legally sound text. 086 2 LexKeyPlan 087 We propose a three-step framework for legal text 088 generation, LexKeyPlan. Unlike traditional mod- 089 els that generate responses directly from context, 090 LexKeyPlan introduces an intermediate planning 091 stage using keyphrases. These keyphrases serve 092 as a forward-looking blueprint, outlining the intent 093 of the future response. By anticipating the neces- 094 sary content, they guide the retrieval of relevant 095 external documents, ensuring that the generated 096 text is both factually accurate and grounded. This 097 approach contrasts with existing retrieval augmen- 098 tation methods, which typically use context alone 099 to retrieve relevant information, potentially limiting 100 the relevance of the retrieved content for response 101 generation, in long form text generation. 102 Formally, let x be the input context. The model 103 first generates a content plan c for the response, 104 which can be represented as p(c | x). This content 105 plan, consisting of keyphrases, succinctly captures 106 the essence of the future response. Then the gener- 107 ated plan c is used as query to retrieve relevant doc- 108 uments d from external knowledge sources. The 109 final response y is produced by conditioning the 110 model on the input context, the content plan and the 111 retrieved documents, represented as p(y | c, p, d). 112 Training the Content Plan Generation Module: 113 We train a language model using the input context 114 followed by the content plan. To obtain the target 115 content plan for each input, we utilize the target 116 response text and extract keyphrases from it. We ex- 117 plore two keyphrase extraction algorithms to create 118 the supervision dataset for training this content plan 119 generation module: TextRank (Mihalcea and Tarau, 120 2004), a graph-based ranking algorithm inspired 121 by PageRank, and KeyBERT (Grootendorst, 2020), 122 leveraging embeddings from pre-trained models. 123 Retriever Module: We investigate two off-the- 124 shelf retrievers: 1) BM25 (Robertson et al., 2004), 125 a sparse lexical-based model, and 2) GTR (Ni et al., 126 2021), an embedding-based dense retriever model 127 built on T5-XXL (Raffel et al., 2020). We provide 128 the concatenated list of keyphrases (content plan) 129 as query to retrieve the relevant documents from 130 datastore, built from ECHR judgement documents. 131 Training the Response Generation Module: The 132 language model is trained using the input con- 133 text, content plan, retrieved relevant documents 134 followed by the target response. Since we do not 135 have a gold-standard content plan or relevant docu- 136 ments for training, we extract keyphrases from the 137 target response to serve as the content plan and use 138 the target response as a query to retrieve pseudo- 139 golden relevant documents. During inference, the 140 model uses the actual generated content plan to 141 retrieve relevant documents. 142 This three-step framework offers controllabil- 143 ity, enabling users to adjust the content plan or 144 retrieved documents to steer the model’s response. 145 3 Experiments 146 3.1 Dataset & Metrics 147 ECHR CaseLaw consists of case judgments heard 148 by the European Court of Human Rights. This plan not only guides to produce 324 coherent response but also the retrieval of relevant 325 documents. LexKeyPlan through its anticipatory 326 planning ensures that the generated text is both 327 contextually coherent and factually accurate. as 328 demonstrated with the ECHR case law corpus. 329 4 Limitations 330 LexKeyPlan currently utilizes a simple content 331 planning approach through keyphrases, guided by 332 algorithms like TextRank and KeyBERT. These 333 algorithms, though effective, were primarily devel- 334 oped for general corpora like news articles, scien- 335 tific papers, and other non-legal texts. They are de- 336 signed to extract keyphrases that are broadly appli- 337 cable but may not fully address the unique require- 338 ments and nuances of legal language and context. 339 Future research could explore advanced keyphrase 340 extraction methods specifically tailored to legal 341 texts, such as Mandal et al. (2017). Such methods 342 could handle the distinct terminology and complex 343 structures characteristic of legal language, improv- 344 ing the relevance and precision of keyphrases used 345 in content planning. 346 More sophisticated content planning approaches 347 could significantly enhance the effectiveness of 348 LexKeyPlan. One promising avenue is the use of 349 graphical representations derived from legal con- 350 cept networks. These networks visually map out 351 legal concepts and their interrelationships, creat- 352 ing a structured framework that can guide content 353 generation. Incorporating a specialized legal the- 354 saurus into the planning process can further refine 355 content generation. A legal thesaurus provides a 356 curated vocabulary of legal terms and concepts, 357 enhancing the precision of keyphrases and improv- 358 ing the contextual relevance of the generated con- 359 tent. Improving the integration of content plans 360 during the text generation phase may also involve 361 adopting constrained decoding techniques. Con- 362 strained decoding methods enforce adherence to 363 predefined content plans, ensuring that the gener- 364 ated text aligns closely with the planned structure 365 and content. This approach can help maintain co- 366 herence and fidelity, reducing deviations from the 367 intended content and improving output quality. 368 Currently, LexKeyPlan’s performance is eval- 369 uated using established metrics like ROUGE, 370 BERTScore, and AlignScore. While these met- 371 rics offer quantitative insights, they may not fully 372 capture the complexities of legal content. Future 373 research could develop domain-specific evaluation 374 metrics tailored to the legal field. Another limita- 375 tion of our study is the absence of direct validation 376 by legal experts in the assessment of outputs, which 377 we could not perform due to lack of access to legal 378 experts. Lastly, while our evaluation was based 379 on the ECHR corpus, future work should extend 380 LexKeyPlan to handle legal texts across different 381 languages and jurisdictions. Adapting keyphrase 382 extraction and content planning processes to ac- 383 commodate diverse legal terminologies and frame- 384 works will enhance the system’s applicability. 385 Ethics Statement 386 The ECHR dataset used in this study is publicly 387 available and widely employed in legal NLP re- 388 search. However, it is important to note that this 389 dataset is not anonymized and contains real names 390 and details of the parties involved in the cases. Al- 391 though we do not foresee direct harm resulting 392 from our experiments, handling such sensitive data 393 necessitates careful consideration of privacy and 394 ethical implications. Researchers must be diligent 395 in protecting individual privacy and managing sen- 396 sitive information responsibly, even when using 397 publicly accessible datasets. 398 LLMs utilized in legal contexts have significant 399 implications for both legal professionals and the 400 public. Despite their advanced capabilities, these 401 models carry inherent risks. They may reproduce 402 and amplify biases inherent in their training data, 403 leading to outputs that reflect historical inequalities 404 or stereotypes. Additionally, LLMs may produce 405 incorrect or misleading information, particularly 406 in complex legal scenarios where precision is es- 407 sential. Our research focuses on enhancing rather 408 than replacing human expertise. It is crucial to ap- 409 ply LLM-generated outputs with careful scrutiny, 410 ensuring that these tools are complemented by thor- 411 ough human oversight and critical evaluation. Puduppully et al. (2019) and Laha et al. 684 (2020) proposed micro-planning strategies, where 685 they first establish a content plan based on a se- 686 quence of records and then generate a summary 687 conditioned on that plan. Similar planning ap- 688 proaches have been explored for entity realization 689 (Puduppully et al., 2019). Additionally, Puduppully 690 and Lapata (2021) advocated for macro-planning as 691 a means of organizing high-level document content, 692 either in text form or within latent space (Pudup- 693 pully et al., 2022). 694 In summarization, various plan representations 695 have been investigated. Narayan et al. (2020) 696 treat step-by-step content selection as a plan- 697 ning component, generating sentence-level plans 698 through extract-then-abstract methods, and even 699 sub-sentence-level plans using elementary dis- 700 course units (Adams et al., 2023). Further re- 701 search by Narayan et al. (2021); Liu and Chen 702 (2021) introduced intermediate plans using entity 703 chains—ordered sequences of entities mentioned in 704 the summary. More recently, Narayan et al. (2023); 705 Huot et al. (2023) conceptualized text plans as a 706 sequence of question-answer pairs, which serve as 707 blueprints for content selection (i.e., what to say) 708 and planning (i.e., in what order) in summarization 709 tasks. 710 Recently, Godbole et al. (2024); Shao et al. 711 (2024) have explored planning-based approaches 712 for text generation in tasks such as expository writ- 713 ing and biographical summaries. However, legal 714 text generation presents unique challenges that re- 715 main unexplored in this context. Unlike traditional 716 QA tasks, which involve focused information- 717 seeking queries, legal text generation requires rea- 718 soning over long, complex case facts to construct 719 well-grounded arguments to derive conclusions. 720 This makes planning particularly valuable, as it can 721 help structure retrieval and generation to ensure 722 coherence, factual consistency, and legal validity. 723 To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has 724 investigated planning-based approaches for legal 725 text generation. 726 B Implementation Details 727 We implemented KeyBERT 1 with n-gram range 728 of (1, 3).
