paper_8: Towards Geo-Culturally Grounded LLM Generations Anonymous ACL submission Abstract Generative large language models (LLMs) 001 have been demonstrated to have gaps in di- 002 verse, cultural knowledge across the globe. 003 We investigate the effect of retrieval aug- 004 mented generation and search-grounding tech- 005 niques on the ability of LLMs to display famil- 006 iarity with a diverse range of national cultures. 007 Speciﬁcally, we compare the performance of 008 standard LLMs, LLMs augmented with re- 009 trievals from a bespoke knowledge base (i.e., 010 KB grounding), and LLMs augmented with re- 011 trievals from a web search (i.e., search ground- 012 ing) on a series of cultural familiarity bench- 013 marks. We ﬁnd that search grounding sig- 014 niﬁcantly improves the LLM performance on 015 multiple-choice benchmarks that test propo- 016 sitional knowledge (e.g., the norms, artifacts, 017 and institutions of national cultures), while KB 018 grounding’s effectiveness is limited by inade- 019 quate knowledge base coverage and a subopti- 020 mal retriever. However, search grounding also 021 increases the risk of stereotypical judgments 022 by language models, while failing to improve 023 evaluators’ judgments of cultural familiarity in 024 a human evaluation with adequate statistical 025 power. These results highlight the distinction 026 between propositional knowledge about a cul- 027 ture and open-ended cultural ﬂuency when it 028 comes to evaluating the cultural familiarity of 029 generative LLMs. 030 1 Introduction 031 Contemporary large language models (LLMs) are pre- 032 trained on huge corpora of natural language text (Rad- 033 ford et al., 2019) and then ﬁne-tuned using human 034 feedback to improve their quality (Bai et al., 2022). 035 During both processes, it is possible for text from a 036 particular culture or cultures to be over-represented in 037 the training data (Dodge et al., 2021) and for the per- 038 spectives, norms, and mores of speciﬁc cultures to be 039 over-represented in the feedback from human evalua- 040 tors (Prabhakaran et al., 2022; Atari et al., 2023). Con- 041 sequently, there is growing recognition of the short- 042 comings of generative LLMs with respect to their abil- 043 ity to represent and serve people of diverse geo-cultural 044 backgrounds at the global scale (Adilazuarda et al., 045 2024; Pawar et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2025). Models 046 tend to stereotype different cultures (Jha et al., 2023; 047 Bhutani et al., 2024), erase and simplify their repre- 048 sentation (Qadri et al., 2025), and provide very lim- 049 ited knowledge and context about artifacts and norms 050 that are salient to them (Myung et al., 2024; Rao et al., 051 2024). Despite these gaps, strategies for intervening 052 and eliciting culturally appropriate content from the 053 models remain under-explored. 054 We study two strategies to improve cultural aware- 055 ness of LLM generation using external knowledge. 056 In the ﬁrst strategy, we construct a bespoke cultural 057 knowledge base (KB) and apply a retrieval augmented 058 generation (RAG) technique (Lewis et al., 2020; Gao 059 et al., 2023) so that the input to the language model 060 includes relevant cultural text from the knowledge 061 base for better generation. In the second strategy, we 062 use a commercially-available search-grounding gener- 063 ation API which translates user prompts into a web 064 search query, uses it to retrieve relevant pieces of text 065 from the Internet, and grounds the LLM generation on 066 the retrieved text. We call these two strategies KB- 067 grounding and search-grounding, respectively. 068 In our experiments, we highlight the necessity of a 069 multi-pronged approach to evaluating cultural aware- 070 ness in language model generations. Speciﬁcally, we 071 leveraged multiple benchmarks (Myung et al., 2024; 072 Rao et al., 2024; Bhutani et al., 2024) to evaluate cul- 073 tural knowledge and the ability to avoid cultural stereo- 074 typing of the models equipped with the two strategies, 075 compared with the vanilla generation baseline. We also 076 conducted a human evaluation of open-ended model 077 responses to various prompts designed to test cultural 078 awareness, wherein evaluators from a speciﬁc national 079 culture rated how well the model’s output reﬂected a 080 culturally informed perspective. The results from both 081 experiments shed light on the pros and cons of the two 082 strategies. Finally, we conclude the paper by discussing 083 key ﬁndings and offering suggestions for future work. 084 2 Improving Cultural Awareness with 085 External Knowledge 086 Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) is a technique 087 for enhancing the quality of large language model gen- 088 eration. To implement RAG, a user prompt is ﬁrst 089 used to retrieve relevant information (e.g., text or doc- 090 uments) from a database, which is then added to the 091 1 prompt before being passed to a generative LLM to 092 produce a grounded response (Lewis et al., 2020; Gao 093 et al., 2023). RAG has shown to be effective in sev- 094 eral applications, particularly those involving tasks the 095 base LLM was not well-trained for such as fact veri- 096 ﬁcation (Asai et al., 2023; Singal et al., 2024; Khaliq 097 et al., 2024) and domain-speciﬁc question answering 098 (QA) (Seo et al., 2024; Xiong et al., 2024; Kim and 099 Min, 2024). Some existing work also creates be- 100 spoke knowledge bases for use with RAG to tailor out- 101 puts to their speciﬁc applications (Sun et al., 2025; 102 Li et al., 2024). Meanwhile, instead of querying a 103 KB, other techniques retrieve external information by 104 searching the internet, which allows access to up-to- 105 date knowledge with high-quality ranking outputs (Fan 106 et al., 2024; Shuster et al., 2022; Lazaridou et al., 2022; 107 Yao et al., 2022; Nakano et al., 2021; Komeili et al., 108 2022). In light of these successes, we study both KB- 109 grounding and search-grounding as techniques for im- 110 proving the cultural awareness of LM generations. 111 2.1 The Knowledge Base Grounding Strategy 112 We compiled culturally salient data from four large 113 sources—CultureAtlas (Fung et al., 2024), Cube (Kan- 114 nen et al., 2024), CultureBank (Shi et al., 2024), and 115 SeeGULL (Jha et al., 2023)—to serve as our knowl- 116 edge base. For each entry in each source, we converted 117 it into into text (if it was not already), embedded it into 118 a vector, and added it to a vector store for querying. 119 Fig. 1 (top) shows how the KB-grounding strategy 120 handles an incoming prompt. First, a query rewriter 121 extracts the important parts of the prompt to form a 122 query. We can conﬁgure this step to test different KB 123 queries (e.g., whether to include choices of a multiple- 124 choice question prompt in the query). Next, we use 125 the query to retrieve n documents from the KB. We 126 optionally check whether each of the documents is in- 127 deed relevant to the original prompt by prompting the 128 base LLM and include only the k relevant ones in the 129 prompt. We call the process with the relevancy check 130 step selective RAG, while non-selective RAG includes 131 all n documents in the prompt. Then, we feed the 132 augmented prompt to the LLM to get a raw answer. 133 For multiple-choice question answering (QA) tasks, we 134 create a manual verbalizer to map the raw answer to 135 one of the choices so that we can compute the model 136 accuracy. In contrast, we use the raw answer as the ﬁnal 137 output for an open-ended generation task. See the Ap- 138 pendix for details about the KB, the queries, the prompt 139 templates, and the implementation. 140 In Section 3, we apply KB-grounding to three dif- 141 ferent LLMs: gemini-ﬂash-1.5 (Gemini) (Team et al., 142 2024), gpt-4o-mini (GPT) (OpenAI et al., 2024) and 143 olmo2-7b (OLMo) (OLMo et al., 2025). 144 2.2 The Search Grounding Strategy 145 Fig 1 (bottom) outlines how the search-grounding strat- 146 egy works. We feed the original prompt to the search- 147 grounding generation API which converts the prompt 148 original prompt Query rewriting query KB vector store n n docs LLM for relevancy check For selective RAG k docs Prompt augmentation augmented  prompt LLM for answer generation raw answer Manual verbalizer For multiple-choice QA final output original prompt Search- grounded LLM raw answer Manual verbalizer final output For multiple-choice QA Internet Knowledge base grounding Search grounding Figure 1: (Top) The knowledge base grounding strat- egy and (Bottom) The search grounding strategy. Dashed boxes indicate optional steps that are executed only under the annotated conditions. For KB ground- ing, the same LLM is used for both relevancy check and answer generation. into a search query, inputs it to a search engine to ob- 149 tain relevant text from the web pages returned by the 150 search, integrates relevant text into the prompt, and 151 then generates a response using an LLM based on the 152 augmented prompt. Thus, the search-grounding strat- 153 egy effectively replaces the bespoke KB in Section 2.1 154 with the entire web, and replaces the vector-based KB 155 querying with retrieving prompt-relevant content with 156 a powerful search engine. 157 We implemented search grounding on Google Ver- 158 tex AI. This enables retrieval of prompt-relevant con- 159 tent from the Google search engine, which is then inte- 160 grated into the prompt that is given to the Gemini LM 161 to generate a response. Search-grounding is not cur- 162 rently available on APIs for accessing GPT or OLMo, 163 so we only implemented search-grounding for Gemini. 164 3 Cultural Competence Benchmarks 165 We evaluated the KB-grounding and search-grounding 166 strategies using multiple-choice cultural QA bench- 167 marks. 168 3.1 Cultural Knowledge 169 Setup. We used two benchmark datasets to test the 170 sensitivity of LLMs with respect to two facets of cul- 171 ture. The ﬁrst, BLEnD, contains questions about ev- 172 eryday cultural knowledge (such as food, sports, fam- 173 2 Figure 2: Performance of all strategies for all models on the BLEnD, NORMAD (Country and Country+Value), and stereotype avoidance benchmarks, with 95% conﬁdence intervals; higher values are better for all plots. ily, and education) in different countries (Myung et al., 174 2024). We used the ~34k English questions from 175 BLEnD that are related to ten countries1 represented 176 in our bespoke KB. The second, NORMAD, focuses 177 on cultural norms and values (Rao et al., 2024). Each 178 question is a story in an everyday scenario, and asks 179 whether a character’s action in the story is socially ac- 180 ceptable within the given context (Yes, No, or Neither). 181 We experimented with two types of contexts – Country 182 and Country+Value. The former speciﬁed a country 183 where the story takes place, while the latter addition- 184 ally indicated the value paradigm the character should 185 adhere to. NORMAD has ~2.6k questions in total. 186 We compared the vanilla generation with the KB- 187 grounding and the search-grounding generations. For 188 KB-grounding, we considered both the selective and 189 non-selective RAG approaches. For BLEnD speciﬁ- 190 cally, because answer choices are potentially relevant 191 to the semantic content of the question, we consid- 192 ered query rewriting both “with choices” and “without 193 choices” included in the KB query. 194 Results. Fig. 2 (left) presents the results of the 195 BLEnD benchmark. A repeated-measures ANOVA 196 revealed a signiﬁcant effect of strategy on accuracy 197 across all three LLMs. However, the optimal meth- 198 ods differed among the LLMs: search-grounding for 199 Gemini, non-selective KB-grounding (without answer 200 choices in KB queries) for GPT, and both selective 201 KB-grounding (with choices in KB queries) and the 202 vanilla approach for OLMo. We also observed the ef- 203 fectiveness of both KB- and search-grounding in sev- 204 eral examples. For instance, the vanilla Gemini incor- 205 rectly answered the question, “What is the most pop- 206 ular sport team in Ethiopia? (A) coffee (B) lg twins 207 (C) persepolis (D) real madrid.” It selected (D), likely 208 due to Real Madrid’s high frequency in the training cor- 209 pora concerning popular sport teams. In fact, the cor- 210 rect answer is (A), as ‘coffee’ refers to the Ethiopian 211 Coffee Sport Club. This information is available on 212 the internet; hence, it is not surprising that search- 213 1China, Ethiopia, Greece, Indonesia, Iran, Mexico, South Korea, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States. grounding correctly answered this question. Notably, 214 search-grounded Gemini achieves 74.2% accuracy for 215 questions related to Ethiopia, signiﬁcantly higher than 216 60.3% of the vanilla baseline and 62.9% of the best KB 217 grounding setting. Certain KB-grounding settings also 218 answered the above question correctly, even though 219 ‘Ethiopian Coffee’ was not mentioned in any of the 220 retrieved texts. The only text retrieved by selective 221 RAG KB-grounding was about sports in Ethiopia in 222 general, which possibly reminded the model to avoid 223 answers from other countries. While this worked, it 224 would be better and more reliable if the knowledge base 225 had wider coverage, including direct information about 226 the Ethiopian Coffee team. 227 The middle two charts in Fig. 2 present the 228 NORMAD benchmark results for both Country and 229 County+Value context types. Consistent with BLEnD, 230 search-grounded Gemini performed best for both con- 231 text types compared to other strategies. For GPT, se- 232 lective KB-grounding outperformed alternatives in the 233 Country context, while the vanilla strategy performed 234 best in the Country+Value context. The trend for 235 OLMo was similar to GPT, except that selective KB- 236 grounding performed comparably to the vanilla for the 237 Country+Value context. We found that KB ground- 238 ing struggled in this task because, several times, the 239 retrieved texts were related to one aspect of the ques- 240 tion but not all. For example, some retrieved texts were 241 about the country but not the exact situation in the ques- 242 tion or vice versa. This could cause the LLMs to give 243 wrong answers. The relevancy check step implemented 244 in selective RAG mitigated this issue, albeit to a limited 245 extent. We posit that a better tuned KB retriever would 246 further address this problem (only if the pertinent fact 247 is present in the KB (Joren et al., 2024)). 248 3.2 Stereotype Avoidance 249 Setup. An important aspect of demonstrating cultural 250 awareness is the avoidance of stereotyping behavior. 251 Hence, we adopted the SeeGULL stereotype avoidance 252 test proposed by Bhutani et al. (2024) to evaluate the 253 studied strategies. Each question asks the model to 254 indicate a person’s nationality based on a stereotype. 255 3 For example, “I know a person who is a ﬁghter. This 256 person is: (A) Albanian (B) Afghan (C) Filipino (D) 257 Guyanese. Write your answer on the next line, or write 258 (?) if you are unsure.” In every question, only one 259 country in the choices is stereotypically associated with 260 the question. However, we considered only ‘(?)’ the 261 correct answer, since it reﬂects the LLM’s ability to 262 avoid stereotypical responses. The benchmark contains 263 ~4.6k questions. As with BLEnD, since the choices 264 may be semantically related to the question, we imple- 265 mented selective and non-selective RAG both with and 266 without answer choices included in the KB query. 267 Results. Fig. 2 (right) shows that, on this benchmark, 268 Gemini vastly outperformed GPT and OLMo in avoid- 269 ing stereotyping, with the vanilla Gemini showing the 270 best performance. However, while all other Gemini 271 methods performed relatively well on this task, search- 272 grounding led to a signiﬁcant degradation in perfor- 273 mance, with the model selecting the stereotypical op- 274 tions considerably more than the vanilla Gemini. This 275 aligns with the thought that internet-sourced informa- 276 tion can reinforce existing biases (Nakano et al., 2021). 277 4 Human Evaluation 278 Setup. To evaluate the strategies on a more open- 279 ended text generation task, we translated ﬁve ques- 280 tions from BLEnD and ﬁve questions from NORMAD 281 into open-ended prompts asking the model to tell a 282 story set in a particular country. We adapted each of 283 these ten questions for the ten national cultures used 284 in the BLEnD benchmark evaluation, leaving us with 285 100 (country, prompt) pairs. Next, we generated re- 286 sponses from Gemini using the vanilla, the selective 287 KB-grounding, and the search-grounding. For each 288 strategy, we generated three unique responses with the 289 temperature of 0.5. Then we recruited nine evaluators 290 from each of the ten studied cultures to rate, on a scale 291 from 0 to 4, how culturally informed each response was 292 and to provide a brief justiﬁcation of their score (see 293 Appendices A.6–A.7 for details). 294 Results. A repeated-measures ANOVA found no sig- 295 niﬁcant effect of strategy on evaluators’ judgments of 296 cultural awareness in model responses (F = .18, p = 297 .827) Also, the interaction effect between an evalua- 298 tor’s national culture and the generation strategy used 299 was not signiﬁcant (F = .84, p = .651). This sug- 300 gests no systematic relationship exists between gener- 301 ation strategies and national cultures in improving the 302 cultural awareness of open-ended model outputs as per- 303 ceived by human evaluators. That said, a qualitative 304 look at some model generations does provide some 305 evidence that both grounding strategies can enhance 306 the cultural speciﬁcity of model outputs. In response 307 to the prompt ‘Tell me a story in Mexico in which a 308 group of people of varying ages eat together and all 309 guests behave in a socially acceptable way,’ the selec- 310 tive KB-grounded and search-grounded responses each 311 mentioned many speciﬁc dishes and games, while the 312 vanilla response was far more generic (see Appendix 313 A.8 for examples). However, search-grounding some- 314 times led Gemini to provide a summary of the content 315 that the prompt asked for a story about (as opposed to 316 actually telling a story), a behavior that evaluators took 317 to warrant low scores for cultural awareness, deﬂating 318 the mean score for search-grounding. All prompts and 319 responses used in this evaluation are available in sup- 320 plementary material along with the data card. 321 5 Discussion and Conclusion 322 This paper studies the effectiveness of the KB ground- 323 ing and the search grounding strategies for improving 324 cultural awareness of LLM generation. We discuss the 325 key ﬁndings and suggestions below. 326 KB Grounding vs Search Grounding. The advan- 327 tages of search-grounding on BLEnD and NORMAD 328 speak to the vast space of cultural facts on the internet. 329 Even the large KB we compiled here still lacked many 330 culturally relevant facts. We also observed some bias 331 in each knowledge source used: approximately 19% of 332 CultureAtlas entries and 25% of CultureBank entries 333 concern the culture of the United States. While the web 334 as a whole remains biased towards Western sources and 335 values (Johnson et al., 2022), it is more likely to contain 336 necessary cultural information due to its sheer scale. 337 However, the poor performance of search-grounding 338 on the stereotype avoidance benchmark reminds us that 339 the context retrieved via web search could reinforce 340 the (typically false) notion that stereotypes are factual 341 and encourage models to afﬁrm those stereotypes. This 342 suggests that search-grounding is yet not a panacea for 343 improving the cultural sensitivity of LLMs. 344 Knowledge vs Fluency. The results of the human 345 evaluation do not show that search-grounding or KB- 346 grounding improved the cultural awareness of LLM 347 outputs. The divergence in the performance of both 348 strategies on the human evaluation and the multiple- 349 choice QA benchmarks suggests that we ought to draw 350 a distinction between two varieties of cultural aware- 351 ness. On the one hand, there is a sense of cul- 352 tural awareness that involves possessing propositional 353 knowledge about a culture (i.e., knowing facts about 354 that culture), as measured by the multiple-choice QA 355 benchmarks, where the grounding strategies can im- 356 prove the model performance. However, another sense 357 of cultural awareness involves writing and speaking 358 like someone with ﬁrst-hand experience of and immer- 359 sion in a culture, i.e., a sense of cultural ﬂuency, as 360 measured by our human evaluation, which revealed that 361 the two grounding strategies was of limited value. We 362 leave it to future work to develop strategies for improv- 363 ing the cultural awareness of generative language mod- 364 els along this second axis. 365 4 Limitations 366 We acknowledge the following limitations of our work 367 in this paper. First, we ran our evaluations only on 368 smaller versions of the GPT-4, Gemini 1.5, and OLMO 369 2 models. It remains an open question whether our pat- 370 tern of results would be similar for larger versions of 371 these models and other model families. Second, for 372 BLEnD and the human evaluation, we ran our evalua- 373 tions using prompts that were relevant to ten national 374 countries and cultures; a more comprehensive study 375 would require the use of a wider range of national and 376 regional cultures. With the momentum in the com- 377 munity to create more culturally salient resources, a 378 more comprehensive study in the future will help iden- 379 tify gaps and interventions for the majority world. Fi- 380 nally, all of our evaluations concerned solely English- 381 language prompts and outputs. While we take it to be 382 an important goal for generative language models that 383 they be able to produce culturally-informed outputs 384 about any culture in the world’s most widely-spoken 385 language, the landscape of cultural awareness becomes 386 much more nuanced when one considers the rich varie- 387 gation that exists in phrasing and dialect across a wide 388 range of languages. We leave it to future work to ex- 389 amine whether the strategies used here can be adapted 390 to a multi-lingual context. 391 Ethical Considerations 392 As generative large language models are developed and 393 deployed rapidly across the globe, it is important to re- 394 ﬂect on how we can improve user experience at a sim- 395 ilar pace. The promise of model utility for a myriad of 396 tasks such as that of a writing assistant, remains unful- 397 ﬁlled if the model is not beneﬁcial or usable for a vast 398 majority. With this work, we attempted to begin adap- 399 tation of techniques in NLP to further the cause of cul- 400 tural awareness and relevance in models. As noted in 401 our limitations, with more comprehensive work across 402 a greater number of cultures and countries, we hope 403 that development of more culturally aware models will 404 be possible. 405 References 406 Muhammad Farid Adilazuarda, Sagnik Mukherjee, 407 Pradhyumna Lavania, Siddhant Shivdutt Singh, Al- 408 ham Fikri Aji, Jacki O’Neill, Ashutosh Modi, and 409 Monojit Choudhury. 2024. We do not interpret these numbers 818 10 literally, rather seeing this as a sign that human gen- 819 erated data may occasionally boost performance to 820 an extent that could be fundamentally unachievable 821 by purely synthetic data. 822 B Related Work 823 Synthetic data usage for Fact Verification and 824 Evidence-Based Question Answering: 825 Human annotation is often the bottleneck in 826 the collection of datasets for Fact Verification and 827 Evidence-Based Question Answering (Liu et al., 828 2022; Schimanski et al., 2024). 829 It is unsurprising, then, that since Language 830 Models have grown powerful enough to produce 831 text output grounded in the input context (Tan et al., 832 2024; Fu et al., 2023; Ouyang et al., 2022; Ashok 833 and Lipton, 2023), there has been an explosion in 834 the usage of synthetic data for FV and QA. 835 Recent works use the method to create bench- 836 mark datasets in a semi-automated (Liu et al., 2022; 837 Ni et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2021) or fully auto- 838 mated (Wan et al., 2024; Muhlgay et al., 2023; 839 Namboori et al., 2024) fashion. 840 Synthetic data generation has also seen increased 841 usage in the approaches to solving the tasks them- 842 selves. The core similarities of these works, be 843 it Natural Language Inference (Ye et al., 2022; 844 Hsieh et al., 2023; Hosseini et al., 2024), Fact Ver- 845 ification / Correction (Tang et al., 2024; Ashok 846 et al., 2023) or Evidence-Based Question Answer- 847 ing, (Puri et al., 2020; Hematian Hemati and Beigy, 848 2024) is the reliance on LMs to generate training 849 data for fine-tuning. This is the paradigm studied 850 in our work, making our analysis applicable to a 851 broad range of recent works in Fact Verification, 852 NLI and Evidence-based Question Answering. 853 Studies on replacing human annotation with 854 synthetic data: 855 The replacement of human annotation with syn- 856 thetic data is extensively studied in the pretraining 857 stage of LMs, where results consistently show (Shu- 858 mailov et al., 2023; Seddik et al., 2024; Guo et al., 859 2023; Briesch et al., 2023) catastrophic forgetting, 860 mode collapse, and performance deterioration. 861 In our setting, relying only on synthetic data 862 still achieves reasonable performance across all 863 tasks. This suggests that the usage of exclusively 864 synthetic data poses fewer risks when generations 865 are grounded in diverse, natural ‘evidence texts.’ 866 Interestingly, conclusions which confirm our 867 findings are found more in the image and multi- 868 modal domains, where recent work (Singh et al., 869 2024; He et al., 2023; Fan et al., 2024) finds that 870 synthetic data holds promise, but must be used in 871 conjunction with human data to mitigate its harms. 872 There is limited work on understanding whether 873 synthetic data can replace human annotation in a 874 task-specific setting for the language domain. Li 875 et al. (2023) categorize text classification tasks by 876 subjectivity, showing that synthetic data is less use- 877 ful when tasks are more subjective. This draws 878 them to focus on different tasks (sentiment classifi- 879 cation, relation extraction and spam detection), and 880 they do not study using a mixture of real and syn- 881 thetic data. Bisbee et al. (2024) demonstrate that 882 replacing political survey respondents with LMs 883 produces unreliable results, while Ahmed et al. 884 (2024) find that there are specific software engi- 885 neering subtasks where synthetic data approaches 886 human performance. Chen et al. (2024) show that 887 instruction-following capabilities are diminished 888 when using synthetic data and present a machine 889 unlearning approach to mitigate this. The diver- 890 sity of results when evaluating the impact of using 891 purely synthetic data confirms that the feasibility 892 of replacing human annotation with synthetic data 893 is highly task dependant. This work deepens our 894 understanding of the problem by being the first to 895 study whether synthetic data can replace human 896 annotation on the fundamental tasks of fact verifi- 897 cation and evidence-based question answering. 898 C Synthetic Data Generation 899 In our implementation (Figure 19), we use few- 900 shot learning with k = 3, i.e., three examples per 901 query, with each example drawn randomly (with 902 replacement) from the training set of the specific 903 dataset. 904 We generate one synthetic point for every real 905 point in the dataset, using the evidence text it is 906 associated with. This gives us a total of n synthetic 907 data points for every n real data points in a dataset. 908 We observed that if we did not correct for la- 909 bel shift, the prompt model would be heavily bi- 910 ased towards True claims, i.e., it would generate a 911 dataset containing 90% True claims, while original 912 datasets have proportions between 33%–60% True. 913 For the synthetic datasets used in our experi- 914 ments, we correct for this label shift by specifying 915 the label of the claim we wish to generate and pro- 916 viding only examples of claims with that specific 917 label in the prompt. 918 11 For all datasets, we verify that the diversity of 919 the generated claims/ questions/ answers are com- 920 parable to that of the human generated texts (see 921 Appendix E) 922 This setting is generous towards synthetic data 923 generation. In practice, we might only have three 924 fixed examples to use in the prompt, potentially 925 reducing the diversity of synthetic data generated. 926 We verify that this does not affect the results of 927 our experiment in the Chain-of-Thought ablation 928 (Figure 15), where we use a fixed set of examples 929 to generate all synthetic data points. paper_10: Learning Auxiliary Tasks Improves Reference-Free Hallucination Detection in Open-Domain Long-Form Generation Anonymous ACL submission Abstract Hallucination, the generation of factually in- 001 correct information, remains a significant chal- 002 lenge for large language models (LLMs), es- 003 pecially in open-domain long-form generation. 004 Existing approaches for detecting hallucination 005 in long-form tasks either focus on limited do- 006 mains or rely heavily on external fact-checking 007 tools, which may not always be available. 008 In this work, we systematically investigate 009 reference-free hallucination detection in open- 010 domain long-form responses. Our findings re- 011 veal that internal states (e.g., model’s output 012 probability and entropy) alone are insufficient 013 for reliably (i.e., better than random guessing) 014 distinguishing between factual and hallucinated 015 content. To enhance detection, we explore vari- 016 ous existing approaches, including prompting- 017 based methods, probing, and fine-tuning, with 018 fine-tuning proving the most effective. To fur- 019 ther improve the accuracy, we introduce a new 020 paradigm, named RATE-FT, that augments fine- 021 tuning with an auxiliary task for the model to 022 jointly learn with the main task of hallucina- 023 tion detection. With extensive experiments and 024 analysis using a variety of model families & 025 datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness and 026 generalizability of our method, e.g., +3% over 027 general fine-tuning methods on LongFact. 028 1 Introduction 029 With the recent advancements in model scale and 030 pretraining data, large language models (LLMs) 031 have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in var- 032 ious natural language processing (NLP) tasks 033 (Brown et al., 2020). Despite these successes, hal- 034 lucination, where models tend to produce content 035 that conflicts with real-world facts, remains a sig- 036 nificant challenge (Zhang et al., 2023). Most ex- 037 isting research on hallucination detection has fo- 038 cused on short-form tasks, where the output con- 039 sists of one or a few tokens. For exam- 268 ple, medical students deepen their understanding 269 of anatomy by studying diagrams, practicing in 270 simulations, and engaging in hands-on dissections, 271 each offering a unique perspective on the same 272 foundational knowledge. For hallucinated claims, we leverage the aug- 289 mented rationale to guide the model in generating 290 an appropriate correct answer along with an expla- 291 nation. After constructing these QA examples, they 292 are combined with the original data for fine-tuning. 293 By integrating these two strategies, we pro- 294 pose Rationale and Auxiliary Task Enhanced Fine- 295 Tuning (RATE-FT) (Figure 1). Our study begins 332 with an analysis of the model’s internal states, 333 demonstrating that these states alone cannot reli- 334 ably detect hallucinations. We then evaluate several 335 existing approaches, including prompting, probing, 336 and fine-tuning, with fine-tuning emerging as the 337 most effective method. A potential improvement could be to ex- 347 plore leveraging the detector’s feedback as a reward 348 signal to guide LLMs to generate more factual re- 349 sponses. Based on whether 583 the hallucinated content contradicts read-world 584 facts or the input context, hallucination can be cat- 585 egorized into two main groups: factuality halluci- 586 nation and faithfulness hallucination (Huang et al., 587 2023). Extensive research has been conducted on 588 exploring the causes (Onoe et al., 2022; Kang and 589 Choi, 2023; Wei et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024), de- 590 tection (Min et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023; Chen 591 et al., 2024a; Fadeeva et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2024), 592 and mitigation (Gao et al., 2023; Ji et al., 2023; Tian 593 et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024b; Kang et al., 2024; 594 Lin et al., 2024) of hallucination in LLMs. How- 595 ever, most existing hallucination detection methods 596 have primarily focused on short-form tasks, where 597 the output consists of one or a few tokens. In this 598 work, we shift the focus to the more challenging 599 problem of reference-free hallucination detection 600 in open-domain long-form generation, where out- 601 puts are substantially longer and require a more 602 nuanced evaluation of actuality. 603 A.3 Benchmark Construction Details 604 For each prompt in the sampled subset (200 605 prompts), we obtain a long-form response from 606 Llama-3-8B-Instruct with greedy decoding. Fol- 607 lowing Wei et al. (2024), we employ the model 608 to decompose long-form responses into atomized 609 claims and assess whether each claim is relevant to 610 answering the corresponding prompt. Claims sup- 614 ported by the search results are labeled as “factual”, 615 while those contradicted by the results are cate- 616 gorized as “hallucinated”. After construction, we 617 obtain 2394 factual claims and 223 hallucinated 618 claims, respectively. A Large Scale Empirical Study across 20 NLP Evaluation Tasks Anonymous ACL submission Abstract There is an increasing trend towards evaluating 001 NLP models with LLMs instead of human 002 judgments, raising questions about the validity 003 of these evaluations, as well as their repro- 004 ducibility in the case of proprietary models. 005 We provide JUDGE-BENCH, an extensible 006 collection of 20 NLP datasets with human an- 007 notations covering a broad range of evaluated 008 properties and types of data, and comprehen- 009 sively evaluate 11 current LLMs, covering both 010 open-weight and proprietary models, for their 011 ability to replicate the annotations. Our evalu- 012 ations show substantial variance across models 013 and datasets. Models are reliable evaluators 014 on some tasks, but overall display substantial 015 variability depending on the property being 016 evaluated, the expertise level of the human 017 judges, and whether the language is human 018 or model-generated. We conclude that LLMs 019 should be carefully validated against human 020 judgments before being used as evaluators. 021 1 Introduction 022 For many natural language processing (NLP) tasks, 023 the most informative evaluation is to ask humans 024 to judge the model output. Such judgments are tra- 025 ditionally collected in lab experiments or through 026 crowdsourcing, with either expert or non-expert 027 annotators, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Recently, there 028 has been a trend towards replacing human judg- 029 ments with automatic assessments obtained via 030 large language models (LLMs) (Chiang and Lee, 031 2023; Wang et al., 2023a; Liu et al., 2023; Li et al., 032 2024; Zheng et al., 2024, inter alia). For exam- 033 ple, the LLM could be instructed to rate a response 034 generated by a dialogue system for its perceived 035 plausibility on a scale from 1 to 5. This drasti- 036 cally reduces the evaluation effort and is claimed 037 to yield more reliable results across multiple eval- 038 uation rounds (Landwehr et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 039 2023b; Reiter, 2024; Dubois et al., 2024). 040 Instruction: On a scale of 1 (very  unlikely) to 5 (very likely), how plausible  is it that the last response belongs to the  dialogue? At the same time, the use of LLMs as judges 041 of linguistic output raises new concerns: LLMs 042 may be prone to errors or systematic biases that 043 differ from those of humans, especially on subtle 044 tasks such as evaluating toxicity, or reasoning. 045 This may distort evaluation results and lead to 046 incorrect conclusions. The problem is aggravated 047 by explicit or implicit data leakage (Balloccu et al., 048 2024), which undermines the ability to make broad, 049 generalisable claims beyond the single specific 050 dataset under analysis. Specifically for closed 051 models such as OpenAI’s GPT series, there are 052 serious reproducibility concerns, as LLMs may be 053 retrained or retired at any time, making subsequent 054 comparisons invalid or impossible. 055 Previous studies offer mixed evidence regarding 056 the reliability of LLM evaluators. Some research 057 concludes that they are effective, correlating well 058 with human judgments (Liu et al., 2023; Zheng 059 et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023; Verga et al., 2024; 060 Törnberg, 2023; Huang et al., 2024; Naismith 061 et al., 2023; Gilardi et al., 2023; Kocmi and Fe- 062 dermann, 2023b), albeit with some caveats (Wang 063 et al., 2023a; Wu and Aji, 2023; Hada et al., 2024; 064 Pavlovic and Poesio, 2024). In some cases, LLM 065 evaluators can also provide pairwise preference 066 1 judgments (Kim et al., 2024; Liusie et al., 2024; Liu 067 et al., 2024a; Park et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2024) or 068 fine-grained evaluation beyond a single score, such 069 as error spans (Fernandes et al., 2023; Kocmi and 070 Federmann, 2023a). In contrast, some studies high- 071 light substantial biases in LLMs’ behaviour as eval- 072 uators, both as compared against human judgments 073 (Koo et al., 2023; Zeng et al., 2024; Baris Schlicht 074 et al., 2024) and through intrinsic analyses (Wang 075 et al., 2023b; Liu et al., 2024b; Stureborg et al., 076 2024). These discrepancies likely stem from the 077 limitations of this previous work, which typically 078 relies on a few datasets and models, often restricted 079 to closed-source proprietary models. 080 In this paper, we examine how well current 081 LLMs can approximate human evaluators on a 082 large scale. We prompt 11 among the most re- 083 cent open-weight and proprietary LLMs to gen- 084 erate judgments on 20 datasets with human an- 085 notations on a wide range of quality dimensions, 086 prompt styles, and tasks. Our evaluation goes be- 087 yond existing work by including a wide variety of 088 datasets that differ in the type of task (e.g., transla- 089 tion, dialogue generation, etc.), the property being 090 judged (e.g., coherence, fluency, etc.), the type of 091 judgments (categorical or graded), and the exper- 092 tise of human annotators (experts or non-experts). 093 We provide JUDGE-BENCH, a benchmark which 094 includes upon release a total of over 70,000 test 095 instances with associated human judgments with 096 an extensible codebase.1 097 Our results indicate that LLMs align well with 098 human judgments on certain tasks, like instruction 099 following. However, their performance is incon- 100 sistent across and within annotation tasks. Elici- 101 tation methods like Chain-of-Thought prompting 102 do not reliably improve agreement, in line with 103 recent findings (Sprague et al., 2024). Some propri- 104 etary models—in particular, GPT-4o—align better 105 to humans, but there is a rather small gap with 106 large open-source models, holding promise for the 107 reproducibility of future evaluation efforts. Alto- 108 gether, at the current stage of LLM development, 109 we recommend validating LLM judges against task- 110 specific human annotations before deploying them 111 for any particular task. 112 2 Construction of JUDGE-BENCH 113 One key feature that differs across the datasets in- 114 cluded in JUDGE-BENCH is the source of the data 115 1https://anonymous.4open.science/r/judge-bench-32CC being evaluated, i.e., whether the items to be judged 116 are generated by a model or produced by humans 117 (Fig. 1). For model-generated items, the goal is to 118 evaluate an NLP system. This includes both classic 119 tasks such as machine translation or dialogue re- 120 sponse generation, as well as less standard tasks for 121 which automation has recently become an option 122 thanks to LLMs, such as the generation of plans or 123 logical arguments. This distinction allows us 126 to understand whether LLMs have a positive bias 127 towards machine-generated outputs—a tendency 128 reported in prior work (Xu et al., 2024). 129 The datasets we consider cover a wide span of 130 properties of interest, ranging from grammaticality 131 and toxicity to coherence, factual consistency, and 132 verbosity, inter alia. The proprietary 231 models GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5 exhibit the high- 232 est scores when evaluating acceptability and ver- 233 bosity, while the two Mixtral open models show 234 the strongest correlations for coherence and con- 235 sistency. Overall, no single model demonstrates a 236 clear superiority over others across all categories; 237 instead, different quality dimensions are better as- 238 sessed by different models. 239 Finally, all models achieve better alignment with 240 human judgments when evaluating human lan- 241 guage than when assessing machine-generated text, 242 both for categorical and graded annotations (see 243 Fig. 6 in App. F). This emphasises the need for cau- 244 tion when using LLMs to automatically evaluate 245 the output of NLP systems. 246 5 Conclusions 247 In response to current trends in evaluation, in this 248 paper we conducted a large-scale study of the corre- 249 lation between human and LLM judgments across 250 20 datasets, considering factors such as the prop- 251 erties being assessed, the expertise level of the hu- 252 man judges, and whether the data is model- or 253 human-generated. On some tasks, such as instruc- 254 tion following and the generation of mathemati- 255 cal reasoning traces, models can be reliably used 256 as evaluators. Overall, however, models’ agree- 257 ment with human judgments varies widely across 258 datasets, evaluated properties, and data sources; 259 and elicitation strategies such as Chain-of-Thought 260 prompting do not consistently improve agreement 261 levels, in line with recent findings (Sprague et al., 262 2024). We recommend validation and calibration of 263 LLMs against task-specific human judgments prior 264 to their deployment as evaluators. To facilitate this 265 process, we release JUDGE-BENCH, a benchmark 266 that enables systematic evaluation across a diverse 267 range of tasks and is easily extensible to include 268 any new task of interest. 269 4 Limitations 270 As pointed out by one of the reviewers, correlation 271 with human judges may not be the most appropri- 272 ate way to validate LLM evaluators. Indeed, if the 273 responses of an LLM were found to contain some 274 harmful bias that does not affect the overall cor- 275 relation or to be systematically aligned with the 276 beliefs of one specific group (without taking into 277 account other perspectives), this would arguably 278 not be a good reason to conclude that LLMs are 279 good evaluators. However, we believe that there 280 are tasks where it is still useful and informative 281 to compare LLM judgments against human ones, 282 especially if human annotations come from experts. 283 The reviewer also highlights the potential dangers 284 of reusing pre-existing tasks and datasets without 285 verifying their quality or how well they reflect ac- 286 tual downstream tasks. While we did our best to 287 select a set of tasks that would be representative 288 and meaningful for the NLP community, we ac- 289 knowledge that there are potential shortcomings 290 (such as data leakage) in using pre-existing tasks 291 and datasets without revalidating them. 292 In contrast to approaches that use LLMs for pair- 293 wise preference evaluation, e.g., PairEval (Park 294 et al., 2024) or JudgeBench (Tan et al., 2024), 295 this paper focuses on evaluating the performance 296 of LLMs on generating judgements for categor- 297 ical or graded responses. We leave extending 298 JUDGE-BENCH to include pairwise preference eval- 299 uation and other recent evaluation methods like 300 Prometheus 2 (Kim et al., 2024) to future work. 301 Finally, our work mostly focuses on English- 302 language datasets—with the exception of datasets 303 focussing specifically on machine-translation out- 304 puts. The Corpus of 758 Linguistic Acceptability (CoLA) consists of 10657 759 sentences from 23 linguistics publications, expertly 760 annotated for acceptability (grammaticality) by 761 their original authors. 762 CoLa-grammar (Warstadt and Bowman, 2020). 763 The dataset consists of a grammatically annotated 764 version of the CoLA development set. Each sen- 765 tence in the CoLA development set is labelled with 766 boolean features indicating the presence or absence 767 of a particular grammatical construction (usually 768 syntactic in nature). Two related sets of features 769 are considered: 63 minor features correspond to 770 fine-grained phenomena, and 15 major features cor- 771 respond to broad classes of phenomena. 772 ToxicChat (Lin et al., 2023). collect binary judg- 773 ments on the toxicity and ‘jailbreaking’ nature 774 (prompt hacks deliberately intended to bypass 775 safety policies and induce models to generate un- 776 safe content) of human prompts to LLMs. While 777 the original dataset contains a mix of human- and 778 automatically-annotated instances, here we only 779 consider the human-annotated prompts. 780 LLMBar (Zeng et al., 2024). LLMBar is a 781 dataset targeted at evaluating the instruction- 782 following abilities of LLMs. Each entry of this 783 dataset consists of an instruction paired with two 784 different outputs, one correctly following the in- 785 struction and the other deviating from it. LLMBar 786 has an adversarial split where deviating outputs 787 are carefully constructed to ‘fool’ LLM-based eval- 788 uators and a natural split where deviating outputs 789 are more naturalistic. 790 Topical Chat and Persona Chat (Mehri and 791 Eskenazi, 2020). These datasets contain hu- 792 man judgments on the quality of machine- and 793 human-generated responses based on the pro- 794 vided dialogue context. The annotated dialogues 795 were selected from Topical Chat (Gopalakrish- 796 nan et al., 2019)—a dataset collecting human- 797 human conversations on provided facts—and Per- 798 sona Chat (Zhang et al., 2018), which contains 799 human-human persona-conditioned conversations. 800 Each response is evaluated on 6 attributes: Under- 801 standable, Natural, Maintains Context, Interesting, 802 Uses Knowledge, and Overall Quality. 803 ROSCOE (Golovneva et al., 2023). collect hu- 804 man judgments assessing the quality of GPT- 805 3’s reasonings. The output reasonings are 806 elicited by inputting GPT-3 with questions selected 807 from 4 commonly used reasoning datasets, i.e., 808 CosmosQA (Huang et al., 2019), DROP (Dua 809 et al., 2019), e-SNLI (Camburu et al., 2018) and 810 GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021). While ROSCOE 811 provides annotations on each step of the reasoning 812 trace, here we only consider the global judgments 813 over the whole reasoning. 814 QAGS (Wang et al., 2020). B Upper Bound Estimation for Model 904 Correlations 905 Whenever multiple human annotations were pub- 906 licly available for a property, we computed upper- 907 bound estimates for the correlations achievable by 908 models. The intuition behind these estimates, bor- 909 rowed from neuroscience (Nili et al., 2014), is 910 that the maximum correlation a model can achieve 911 with aggregated human responses is bounded by 912 the average correlation between single-participant 913 responses and the aggregated responses across 914 participants. We applied a similar logic to the 915 human judgments used in the present study and 916 combined it with a bootstrapping approach. For 917 each annotated property, we bootstrapped single- 918 participant responses by sampling 1000 times from 919 the available human responses, excluding data 920 points where a single annotation was available. 921 Next, we computed the alignment between each 922 of the bootstrapped-participant arrays and the array 923 of aggregated responses. Alignment was computed 924 as Spearman’s correlation for graded judgments 925 and Cohen’s kappa for categorical judgments. Fi- 926 nally, we estimated the upper bound as the average 927 of the 1000 alignment measures. In cases where 928 alignment between bootstrapped and aggregated 929 responses could not be computed—because the 930 variance of the bootstrapped responses was null— 931 values were replaced with an average of the ‘non- 932 nan’ correlations. 933 We emphasise that these upper bounds are esti- 934 mates and, as such, are subject to errors. Therefore, 935 it may happen that model performance exceeds 936 these upper bounds. 937 C Inference Details 938 All open-model checkpoints were obtained using 939 the HuggingFace pipeline and we access all pro- 940 prietary models using their corresponding API li- 941 braries. paper_14: Revisiting Uncertainty Quantification Evaluation in Language Models: Spurious Interactions with Response Length Bias Results Anonymous ACL submission Abstract Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) in Language 001 Models (LMs) is crucial for improving their 002 safety and reliability. Evaluations often use 003 performance metrics like AUROC to assess 004 how well UQ methods (e.g., negative sequence 005 probabilities) correlate with task correctness 006 functions (e.g., ROUGE-L). In this paper, we 007 show that commonly used correctness func- 008 tions bias UQ evaluations by inflating the per- 009 formance of certain UQ methods. We evaluate 7 010 correctness functions—from lexical-based and 011 embedding-based metrics to LM-as-a-judge ap- 012 proaches—across 4 datasets × 4 models × 6 013 UQ methods. Our analysis reveals that length 014 biases in the errors of these correctness func- 015 tions distort UQ assessments by interacting 016 with length biases in UQ methods. We identify 017 LM-as-a-judge approaches as among the least 018 length-biased choices and hence a potential so- 019 lution to mitigate these biases. 020 1 Introduction 021 Language Models (LMs) excel at natural language 022 generation but often produce factually incorrect 023 outputs, or “hallucinations” (Guerreiro et al., 2023; 024 Huang et al., 2025). These hallucinations are typ- 025 ically associated with high uncertainty about the 026 correct output (Xiao and Wang, 2021), leading to 027 the emergence of Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) 028 methods as a compelling approach to detect errors 029 (Farquhar et al., 2024; Baan et al., 2023). Since of- 030 ten no ground truth measure for uncertainty exists, 031 evaluation in benchmarks is typically performed us- 032 ing UQ performance metrics like AUROC, which 033 measure how well UQ methods distinguish correct 034 from incorrect answers: if a model is well cali- 035 brated, low uncertainty should correlate with cor- 036 rectness. Consequently, accurately determining 037 correctness in a given generative task is crucial as 038 any inaccuracies can severely compromise UQ per- 039 formance evaluation. 040 Since the UQ performance metric relies on both 041 the UQ method under consideration and the cor- 042 rectness function, errors in either can distort the fi- 043 nal evaluation. If the correctness function is unre- 044 liable, it can mislabel answers, leading to further 045 inaccurate uncertainty assessments. Further, con- 046 founding factors—external variables that simulta- 047 neously affect both scores—can introduce biases, 048 distorting the evaluation. 049 In this paper, we critically analyze the impact of 050 the correctness function on UQ performance met- 051 rics. Specifically, we test 7 different correctness 052 functions, including lexical-based metrics (e.g., 053 ROUGE metrics), embedding-based metrics (e.g., 054 BERTScore (Zhang et al., 2020a)), and LM-as- 055 a-judge approaches (Zheng et al., 2024) across 4 056 datasets × 4 models × 6 UQ methods. Our find- 057 ings reveal two key issues: (i) the correctness func- 058 tion choice significantly impacts UQ results, rais- 059 ing concerns about UQ benchmarks’ reliability, 060 and (ii) widely used lexical-based and embedding- 061 based correctness functions (Farquhar et al., 2024; 062 Fadeeva et al., 2023) introduce systematic biases 063 that distort the performance of certain UQ methods. 064 A human evaluation of 450 LM samples, with 065 four annotations per sample, reveals that this bias 066 stems from confoundedness, that is the mutual de- 067 pendence of certain UQ methods and the errors of 068 certain correctness functions on the output length. 069 Building on this, we identify correctness functions 070 that mitigate bias by avoiding such confounding, 071 finding LM-as-a-judge approaches best suited for 072 UQ evaluation and most aligned with human judg- 073 ment. Overall, this study highlights widespread pit- 074 falls in UQ evaluation and charts a path toward a 075 more reliable evaluation protocol. 076 2 Evaluating uncertainty 077 Here, we review common UQ methods, correctness 078 functions and UQ performance metrics. 079 1 2.1 UQ methods 080 Given an input x to an LM, which generates an 081 output sequence ˆy, a UQ method estimates a mea- 082 sure of the model’s uncertainty about ˆy, denoted 083 as ˆg(ˆy, x). These methods can be broadly catego- 084 rized into three types: (i) single-sample, (ii) multi- 085 sample, and (iii) learned. One simple single-sample 086 approach is negative sequence probability, 087 ˆg(ˆy, x) = −ˆp(ˆy|x) = −QL i=1 ˆp(ˆyi|ˆy<i, x), (1) 088 where L is the length of the generated answer and 089 ˆp the output probabilities assigned by the model. 090 Note that Eq. 1 increases with L. Multiple-sample 091 approaches derive uncertainty scores by sampling 092 multiple responses for the same input x and mea- 093 suring a metric (e.g., variance) across samples. No- 094 tably, several UQ methods in this second group, like 095 Naïve Entropy (Farquhar et al., 2024), use Eq. 1 096 to compute the probability of a sequence of gener- 097 ated tokens. Lastly, learned methods train a binary 098 classifier via supervised learning on a correctness- 099 labeled dataset (Kadavath et al., 2022). We refer 100 readers to App. A for more details on each family. 101 2.2 Correctness functions 102 Correctness functions ˆh(ˆy, x, y) compare a gener- 103 ated answer ˆy to a reference answer y to estimate a 104 correctness score, and can be categorized as lexical- 105 based, embedding-based, or LM-as-a-judge. 106 Lexical-based Correctness functions such as 107 SQuAD (Rajpurkar et al., 2016) and ROUGE vari- 108 ants (Lin, 2004), are based on lexical overlap be- 109 tween ˆy and y. While limitations of these met- 110 rics have been studied in areas like summarization 111 and Question Answering (QA) (Guo and Vosoughi, 112 2023; Chen et al., 2019; Cohan and Goharian, 2016; 113 Fabbri et al., 2021; Reiter and Belz, 2009), their im- 114 pact on UQ evaluation remains largely unexplored. 115 Embedding-based Correctness functions assess- 116 ing similarity by encoding both ˆy and y using a 117 language model, typically BERT-based. Exam- 118 ples include BERTScore (Zhang et al., 2020b) 119 and SentenceBERT cosine similarity (Reimers and 120 Gurevych, 2019). 121 LM-as-a-judge Correctness functions evaluat- 122 ing correctness by using another LM to judge the 123 accuracy of ˆy against y. While ROUGE-L (Recall) is 284 inherently independent of the generated answer’s 285 length, it offers lower correlation with human judg- 286 ment, offering a higher likelihood of additional con- 287 founding variables. For example, it is vulnerable to 288 exploitation by models that produce multiple off- 289 target answers alongside the correct one. 290 4 Conclusion 291 The choice of correctness function heavily influ- 292 ences evaluation of UQ performance metrics, of- 293 ten introducing biases that distort results and com- 294 promise benchmark integrity. Our study exposes 295 these biases, particularly in lexical and embedding- 296 based correctness functions, and shows that LM-as- 297 a-judge provides more reliable assessments. This 298 work underscores the critical role of metric selec- 299 tion in ensuring accurate UQ evaluation. 300 4 Limitations 301 In this work, we have critically examined the role 302 of the correctness function in the evaluation of UQ 303 methods using UQ performance metrics. While 304 our analysis sheds light on biases introduced by 305 correctness functions, certain limitations remain. 306 Our analysis is focused on the context of QA, 307 as it is a standard task in UQ literature and pro- 308 vides well-defined single-answer questions, mak- 309 ing the definition of a correctness function easier 310 compared to open-ended tasks like machine trans- 311 lation and summarization where even objective hu- 312 man judgment of correctness is difficult. However, 313 previous work suggests that the length bias of er- 314 rors in correctness functions is not unique to the 315 QA setting (Guo and Vosoughi, 2023), suggesting 316 that UQ performance metrics will face similar is- 317 sues in such tasks. 318 Our recommendation is to use LM-as-a-judge as 319 a potential correctness function. While using an- 320 other LM to judge correctness has demonstrated 321 advantages (Zheng et al., 2024), it also comes with 322 known limitations (Wang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 323 2024b). The reliability of the correctness assess- 324 ment may vary depending on the choice of the judg- 325 ing LM and the prompt formulation. More concern- 326 ingly, if the same LM is used as both the correct- 327 ness function and as part of the UQ method, we are 328 likely to have correlations between the LM-as-a- 329 judge’s errors and the UQ method, which could in- 330 flate the UQ method’s performance—although this 331 is mitigated by the relatively low frequency of such 332 errors. Additionally, while our analysis on QA is 333 based on widely used QA datasets, we do not know 334 whether the same LM judge and prompts would 335 generalize effectively to other tasks and datasets. 336 Ideally, an LM judge should be rigorously evalu- 337 ated against human annotators before being em- 338 ployed in new tasks and datasets (Bavaresco et al., 339 2024). Furthermore, LM-as-a-judge introduces sig- 340 nificant computational overhead compared to tradi- 341 tional correctness functions, making it less practi- 342 cal for resource-constrained applications. 343 Finally, our study identifies response length as a 344 confounding factor in UQ benchmarking, but other 345 latent variables may also influence UQ methods 346 and correctness functions in subtle ways, as dis- 347 cussed in App. C. A deeper understanding of these 348 biases is crucial for refining UQ evaluation pro- 349 tocols and ensuring more reliable assessments of 350 model uncertainty. 351 References 352 Lukas Aichberger, Kajetan Schweighofer, and Sepp 353 Hochreiter. 2024. These approaches can be broadly 613 classified into three main categories: 1) Single- 614 sample methods: methods that require a single 615 forward pass from the model and that generally 616 use directly the logits and probability distributions 617 over the vocabulary space provided as output from 618 the model; 2) Multiple-sample methods: methods 619 that, given a prompt x, sample multiple possible 620 outputs for the same prompt and compute an un- 621 certainty score based on these outputs; 3) Learned 622 methods: usually probes or small networks directly 623 trained to predict the accuracy of the model given 624 the prompt and the answer. 625 We denote with x the sequence of tokens cor- 626 responding to the prompt. This usually includes 627 the instruction prompt (e.g., "Answer the following 628 7 question") together with the question and additional 629 context. The L generated tokens are indicated as ˆyi. 630 Additionally, a superscript ˆy(s) is used for multiple- 631 sample methods to indicate the s-th sample (out of 632 SUQ samples) sampled for a given prompt. ˆp(·) de- 633 notes the probability assigned by the model. 634 Single-sample methods. Single-sample methods 635 estimate the uncertainty score using the logits that 636 the models output. These logits are usually com- 637 puted on the greedy decoded output or on a low- 638 temperature sample decoded from the model given 639 the prompt x. 640 Negative Sequence Probability. Sequence 641 probability computes the cumulative probability of 642 the sequence. This can be used as an uncertainty 643 score by flipping the sign and considering −ˆp(ˆy|x). 644 When evaluated on the greedy decoding samples, 645 this method is sometimes referred to in the liter- 646 ature as Maximum Sequence Probability (MSP) 647 (Fadeeva et al., 2023; Vashurin et al., 2025). Aich- 648 berger et al. (2024) investigate the difference be- 649 tween the performance of MSP estimated using the 650 greedy decoding and estimated using Beam Search 651 decoding algorithm, which yields sequences with 652 higher likelihood. 653 ˆp(ˆy|x) = L Y i=1 ˆp(ˆyi|ˆy<i, x). (4) 654 Perplexity. Perplexity computes the uncer- 655 tainty score via the exponential of the mean token 656 likelihood (Bahl et al., 1983). Compared to se- 657 quence probability, perplexity normalizes the un- 658 derlying probability by the number of the gener- 659 ated tokens, 660 exp   −1 L L X i=1 log ˆp(ˆyi|ˆy<i, x) ! . (5) 661 Mean Token Entropy. Mean token entropy 662 (Fomicheva et al., 2020; Malinin and Gales, 2020) 663 computes the mean of the per-token entropies over 664 the vocabulary distribution, 665 HT (ˆy, x) = 1 L L X i=1 H [ˆp(ˆyi|ˆy<i, x)] . (6) 666 Multiple-Sample methods. Multiple-sample 667 methods compute an uncertainty score by sam- 668 pling SUQ times for a single prompt. Since it is 669 accessing (more of) the full probability distribu- 670 tion, this class of methods should provide better 671 uncertainty scores than single-sample methods, 672 albeit at the expense of an increased computational 673 cost at inference time. The exact number of sam- 674 ples SUQ is a hyperparameter that usually depends 675 on the specific UQ method. 676 Naive Entropy. Naive Entropy computes the 677 entropy over the different generated samples. The 678 sequence probability of each generation is com- 679 puted using the chain rule of probability, like in the 680 Sequence Probability method, 681 − SUQ X s=0 ˆp(ˆy(s)|x) log ˆp(ˆy(s)|x). (7) 682 Learned methods. Learned methods leverage 683 the model’s internal activations or its entire archi- 684 tecture to train additional networks or classifiers 685 that predict the correctness of the answer. 686 Probes are the most common form of learned 687 method. The most prominent variety of probe is 688 P(IK), also known as P(I Know) (Kadavath et al., 689 2022), which finetunes the entire model to predicts 690 a binary score whether the model can answer the 691 question correctly or not. This is accomplished by 692 attaching a classifier to the embedding of the final 693 token in the last layer. The training set is collected 694 by labeling some generations from the model with 695 the task correctness function. In this paper, we fol- 696 low the implementation of (Farquhar et al., 2024; 697 Kapoor et al., 2024) that does not train the full 698 model but just a logistic regression classifier on top 699 of the representation of the final answer token as in 700 (Chen et al., 2024a). We trained probes using two 701 different correctness functions: LM-as-a-judge (us- 702 ing Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct), and ROUGE- 703 L (Recall) with a 0.5 threshold. When reporting 704 results, we specify the correctness function used 705 to label the dataset and train the probe in round 706 brackets—for example, Probe(LM-as-a-judge), 707 where LM-as-a-judge denotes the judging model. 708 Probes are trained until convergence on each train- 709 ing dataset with L-BFGS and a tolerance value of 710 0.0001 and maximum number of optimization iter- 711 ations of 10000. 712 B Details of Correctness functions 713 In this section, we describe in detail the correctness 714 functions used in our experiments. Many of these 715 metrics return a continuous score, which is bina- 716 rized for calculating AUROC; we detail the thresh- 717 olds t used in this binarization below. 718 8 B.1 Lexical-based 719 Lexical-based metrics assess similarity by measur- 720 ing lexical overlap between the generated sentence 721 and the ground truth. These metrics are among the 722 most widely used due to their low computational 723 cost and long-standing history in QA evaluation. 724 It is important to note that these metrics were 725 originally used to evaluate QA in trained sys- 726 tems, where the output distribution of generated 727 sequences has been aligned with the expected dis- 728 tribution of ground-truth answers in the dataset. 729 However, in common LM zero-shot evaluation set- 730 tings, this alignment is no longer guaranteed. Con- 731 sequently, these metrics may fail to accurately as- 732 sess correctness, requiring careful consideration 733 when applying them. While techniques like incor- 734 porating few-shot examples, as demonstrated by 735 Farquhar et al. (2024), can mitigate this issue to 736 some extent, this does not fully address the funda- 737 mental limitations of lexical-based metrics. 738 ROUGE-L. ROUGE-L measures the longest 739 common subsequence (LCS) between the gener- 740 ated response and the reference answer, allowing 741 for non-contiguous matches (Lin, 2004). In UQ the 742 F1-score (ROUGE-L (F1)) of this metric is typi- 743 cally used, balancing precision and recall (Fadeeva 744 et al., 2023; Kuhn et al., 2023; Duan et al., 2024; 745 Chen et al., 2024a; Qiu and Miikkulainen, 2024; 746 Aichberger et al., 2025). ROUGE-L (Precision) 747 measures the ratio of the longest common subse- 748 quence (LCS) length to the number of unigrams in 749 the generated answer. ROUGE-L (Recall) measures 750 the ratio of the LCS length to the number of uni- 751 grams in the reference answer. ROUGE-L (F1) is 752 the harmonic mean of ROUGE-L precision and re- 753 call. It is important to note that ROUGE-L recall is 754 not affected by the length of the generated answer, 755 whereas precision and F1 metrics are influenced 756 by it. In the experiments of this paper, we con- 757 sider ROUGE-L (F1) and ROUGE-L (Recall) vari- 758 ants, with both metrics computed using the Python 759 package rouge_scorer. Both ROUGE-L variants 760 return continuous scores; where a binary score is 761 used, we consider thresholds t ∈{0.1, 0.3, 0.5} for 762 ROUGE-L (F1), and t = 1.0 for ROUGE-L (Re- 763 call). 764 ROUGE-1. ROUGE-1 measures the unigrams 765 overlap between the generated response and the 766 ground truth (Lin, 2004). ROUGE-1 captures sim- 767 ilarity based on single-tokens overlap. This met- 768 ric has been widely used in QA evaluations and in 769 UQ benchmarks in Aichberger et al. (2025). As 770 in Aichberger et al. (2025), we use the F1 variant 771 (ROUGE-1 (F1)). In the experiments of this paper, 772 the metric has been computed using the Python 773 package rouge_scorer. ROUGE-1 (F1) returns 774 continuous scores; where a binary score is used, 775 we use a threshold t = 0.1. 776 SQuAD. This metric has been introduced in Ra- 777 jpurkar et al. (2016) to measure the performance of 778 systems trained on the homonymous dataset. The 779 metric computes the F1 score based on word over- 780 lap between the prediction and ground truth, treat- 781 ing them as unordered bags of tokens, selecting the 782 highest F1 among multiple references per question, 783 and averaging across all questions. This metric has 784 been used to evaluate correctness for UQ bench- 785 marks in Farquhar et al. (2024). To compute the 786 metric we used the implementation from Von Werra 787 et al. (2022). SQuAD returns continuous scores; 788 where a binary score is used, we use a threshold 789 t = 0.3. 790 B.2 Embedding-based 791 Embedding-based metrics assess similarity by en- 792 coding both the ground truth and generated text 793 using a neural model, typically BERT-based. The 794 goal is to measure semantic similarity rather than 795 surface-level overlap. 796 BERTScore. BERTScore (Zhang et al., 2020b) 797 evaluates generated answers by embedding both the 798 generated text and the ground truth using a BERT 799 pretrained model. It then computes the pairwise 800 cosine similarity between tokens. For each token 801 in the generated text, the highest similarity score 802 with any token in the reference text is selected. Fi- 803 nally, precision, recall, and F1-score are calculated, 804 with the F1-score commonly used in UQ to bal- 805 ance precision and recall. This metric has been 806 used to evaluate correctness for UQ benchmarks in 807 Fadeeva et al. (2023). In the experiments of this pa- 808 per, the metric has been computed using the Python 809 package bert_score as in Fadeeva et al. (2023). 810 BERTScore returns continuous scores; where a bi- 811 nary score is used, we use a threshold t = 0.8, 812 which we empirically found to yield the highest 813 agreement with human raters in Figure 2. 814 SentenceBERT Similarity. A SentenceBERT 815 model (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) is used to 816 encode both the generated answer and the ground 817 truth answer. Specifically, following Chen et al. 818 9 (2024a), nli-roberta-large1 has been used. The 819 cosine similarity is then calculated between the 820 ground truth and generated answer embeddings. 821 This metric has been used to evaluate correct- 822 ness for UQ benchmarks in Chen et al. (2024a). 823 SentenceBERT returns continuous scores; where 824 a binary score is used, we use a threshold t ∈ 825 {0.4, 0.9}. 826 B.3 LM-as-a-judge methods 827 LM-as-a-judge metrics evaluate correctness by us- 828 ing another LM to judge the accuracy of a gener- 829 ated answer against the reference answer from the 830 dataset. The evaluating LM may be specifically 831 trained for this task or not. 832 AlignScore. AlignScore is a metric designed to 833 evaluate the factual consistency of generated text 834 with respect to a ground truth answer (Zha et al., 835 2023). It employs a RoBERTa model trained to as- 836 sess the alignment between two text pieces, deter- 837 mining how well the generated content corresponds 838 to the source information. The training process in- 839 tegrates data from several NLP tasks—natural lan- 840 guage inference, question answering, paraphras- 841 ing, fact verification, information retrieval, seman- 842 tic similarity, and summarization—resulting in a 843 model trained specifically to evaluate correctness. 844 This metric has been used to evaluate correct- 845 ness for UQ benchmarks in Vashurin et al. (2025). 846 AlignScore returns continuous scores; where a bi- 847 nary score is used, we use a threshold t = 0.5. 848 LM-as-a-judge. LM-as-a-judge (Zheng et al., 849 2024) encompasses a set of approaches that rely 850 on a large language model to provide a human- 851 like assessment of generated content by compar- 852 ing it against a reference answer. Generally, dif- 853 ferent prompting strategies can be applied to guide 854 the evaluation process. In our experiments, we 855 used the same prompt as Farquhar et al. (2024) 856 with Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct as the judging 857 model. LM-as-a-judge returns binary scores, so no 858 thresholds are used. 859 1https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/nli- roberta-large C Impact of Correlated and Uncorrelated 860 Errors in the Correctness function on 861 AUROC Estimation 862 In this section, we analyze the impact of correlated 863 or uncorrelated errors in the correctness function 864 on AUROC estimation. 865 Let ˆgi ≡ˆg(ˆyi, xi) ∈R be the uncertainty (UQ) 866 score assigned to the answer ˆyi given the question 867 xi. (8) 894 All terms {TPR, TNR, FPR, FNR} in Eq. 8 are 895 constant properties of the correctness function ˆh, 896 and do not depend on the UQ method ˆg. In this uncorrelated setting, the 900 bias introduced by ˆh does not depend on the UQ 901 metric ˆg. Consequently, while the estimated AU- 902 ROC values will be inaccurate, the ranking of UQ 903 methods by \ AUROC(ˆg) will, in expectation, match 904 the ranking by AUROC(ˆg), provided TPR·TNR > 905 FPR · FNR. In practice, finite-sample effects can 906 lead to variance, but with appropriate sample sizes, 907 comparisons based on \ AUROC(ˆg) remain valid. 908 C.2 Case 2: Correlated errors 909 Analysis ˆhi ̸⊥⊥ˆgi | hi.
