Anonymous ACL submission Abstract 001 The evaluation of text generated by large lan- 002 guage models (LLMs) remains a challenge for 003 question answering, retrieval augmented gener- 004 ation (RAG), summarization, and many other 005 natural language processing tasks. Evaluat- 006 ing the factuality of LLM-generated responses 007 is particularly important in medical question 008 answering, where the stakes are high. One 009 method of evaluating the factuality of text is 010 through the use of information nuggets (answer 011 keys). Nuggets are text representing atomic 012 facts that may be used by an assessor to make 013 a binary decision as to whether the fact repre- 014 sented by said nugget is contained in an answer. 015 Although manual nugget extraction is expen- 016 sive and time-consuming, recent RAG shared 017 task evaluations have explored automating the 018 nuggetization of text with LLMs. In this work, 019 we explore several approaches to nugget gener- 020 ation for medical question answering and eval- 021 uate their alignment with expert human nugget 022 generation. We find providing an example and 023 extracting nuggets from an answer to be the 024 best approach to nuggetization. While, overall, 025 we found the capabilities of LLMs to distill 026 atomic facts limited, Llama 3.3 performed the 027 best out of the models we tested. 028 1 Introduction 029 Evaluation of automatically generated answers is a 030 major bottleneck in the development of question- 031 answering approaches. Although a need for new 032 evaluation approaches was noticed as soon as the 033 system-generated answers became more complex 034 and abstract (Chen et al., 2019), to date, there 035 are no widely accepted evaluation metrics to ap- 036 proximate human judgments on the quality and 037 other aspects of the generated answers. The TREC 038 2024 Retrieval Augmented Generation track eval- 039 uation (Pradeep et al., 2024) revisited the nugget- 040 based evaluation originally developed for judging 041 answers to definition questions in the 2003 ques- 042 tion answering track (Voorhees, 2004). Briefly, a 043 nugget-based evaluation is a two-step process. In 044 the first step, the assessors create a list of atomic 045 facts (nuggets) that must be present in an answer 046 for the answer to be judged correct and complete. 047 In the second step, the assessors manually map 048 each statement in a system-generated answer to 049 the nuggets. Various performance metrics may be 050 then computed. For example, the TREC 2024 RAG 051 track labeled nuggets as supported, partially sup- 052 ported, or not supported by the answer and then 053 computed the system scores by summing the scores 054 of all nuggets and dividing the sum by the number 055 of nuggets. Most importantly, the evaluation has 056 shown correlations between scores derived from an 057 automatic nugget evaluation and a manual nugget 058 evaluation. This supports the belief that LLMs can 059 be used to support evaluations as long as LLMs are 060 not generating the ground truth (Soboroff, 2024). 061 To that end, we explore various approaches to the 062 first step of the evaluation - LLMs’ ability to gener- 063 ate atomic factual statements (cf. Table 1). This is 064 particularly important in medical question answer- 065 ing, where, although infrequently, as demonstrated 066 by the results of the 2024 TREC BioGen track eval- 067 uation, generated answers may contain inappro- 068 priate and potentially harmful information (Gupta 069 et al., 2024). 070 The contributions of this work are as follows: 071 • We manually generate nuggets for the 2024 072 BioGen track topics. 073 • We propose a series of automated nugget- 074 generation approaches considering the ques- 075 tion, answer, and relevant documents. 076 • We evaluated the capabilities of LLMs’ to gen- 077 erate nuggets. 078 Related work: Nugget generation could be 079 viewed as a form of outline generation in two dif- 080 ferent settings: 1) a model or a person generating 081 the nuggets has access to a set of answers or docu- 082 1 Query: "What will mutation in runx2 affect in the future?" Answer: "The effect of the runx2 mutation depends on the kind of the mutation. This gene mostly af- fects bone development. Mutations can cause bone deformities, height lower than expected, extra teeth and other dental problems..." Manually Extracted Nuggets: 1. Affects (runx2 mutation, bone development) 2. Cause (runx2 mutation, bone deformities) 3. Cause (runx2 mutation, height lower than ex- pected) 4. Cause (runx2 mutation, extra teeth) 5. Cause (runx2 mutation, dental problems) ... LLM (Llama 3.3) Generated Nuggets: 1. Runx2 mutation affects bone development 2. Runx2 mutation can cause bone deformities 3. Runx2 mutation can result in lower than ... 4. Runx2 mutation can lead to extra teeth 5. Runx2 mutation can cause other dental problems Table 1: An example of nuggets extracted by a human and LLM for the same query and answer pair. ments containing information needed to generate 083 the answer; 2) the model or person are provided 084 only with the question and have to generate the 085 outline using their background knowledge. While, 086 to the best of our knowledge, work on direct nugget 087 generation is limited to the above RAG evaluation 088 and an evaluation in which the initial set of test 089 nuggets is generated using ChatGPT (Dietz, 2024; 090 Farzi and Dietz, 2024), the related work on out- 091 line generation includes story generation (Wang 092 and Kreminski, 2024) and natural language out- 093 line for code generation (Shi et al., 2024). For 094 medical question answering, nugget-based evalu- 095 ation was revisited in the evaluation of answers 096 to questions about COVID-19 asked by patients 097 and clinicians (Goodwin et al., 2022). The nuggets 098 were generated manually in this evaluation. 099 2 Methods 100 2.1 Manual Nugget Generation 101 For the purpose of having ground truths to eval- 102 uate LLM generated nuggets against, we provide 103 expert-curated, manually generated nuggets for the 104 2024 BioGen track topics. Nuggets were captured 105 from 40 ground truth answers. Each nugget was 106 captured as a semantic triplet in Predicate (subject, 107 object) form. Nuggets were identified by manually 108 assessing the atomic facts represented in each sen- 109 tence and their corresponding predicate, subject, 110 and object. Some sentences may contain multiple 111 atomic facts, for example, sentences comprising 112 multiple phrases conjoined by a coordinating con- 113 junction or lists. In such cases, the semantic triple 114 is identified for each phrase or item in the list and 115 recorded separately. Predicates were normalized 116 across the dataset by mapping to a list of expert- 117 curated predicates deemed to be complete in their 118 coverage of the dataset and in conveying repre- 119 sented facts. Each medical concept contained in 120 either the subject or object was associated with 121 a Concept Unique Identifier (CUI) from the Uni- 122 fied Medical Language System (UMLS) (Lindberg 123 et al., 1993). These associations were made by 124 manually assessing the closest match, if any, from 125 the UMLS Metathesaurus Browser. Some facts 126 required more complex nugget structures includ- 127 ing, but not limited to, "if, then" clauses and com- 128 parisons. These nuggets preserve the underlying 129 logical structure from the answer. We generated 130 a total of 498 nuggets from 40 question-answer 131 pairs which has an average of 12.45 nuggets. Each 132 nugget was reviewed by at least two reviewers. 133 2.2 LLM-based Nugget Generation 134 Model Architectures: We tested both pop- 135 ular open-source and proprietary models for 136 nugget generation. The list of models includes 137 Llama (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Gemma (Riviere 138 et al., 2024), Mistral (Jiang et al., 2023), Phi (Ab- 139 din et al., 2024), Qwen (Qwen et al., 2025), Vi- 140 cuna (Chiang et al., 2023), Falcon (Almazrouei 141 et al., 2023), DeepSeek (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025), 142 and GPT (OpenAI et al., 2024). For some fami- 143 lies of models, we included both larger and smaller 144 versions. 145 Generation Strategies: We developed extensive 146 strategies to generate the nuggets by considering 147 different inputs to the LLMs. specifically, we used 148 questions, reference answers, and cited documents 149 provided for each assertion in the reference answer. 150 We instructed the models to generate the appropri- 151 ate nuggets. The detailed strategies are as follows: 152 (1) Question: In the first strategy, we only pro- 153 vide the question to the LLMs and instruct them to 154 generate all pertinent nuggets that directly address 155 the user’s query. We started with the zero-shot 156 approach and extended our experiments to the few- 157 shot approach to enable in-context learning, where 158 2 we provide an example question and corresponding 159 nuggets in the prompt to direct the model toward 160 better performance. For 265 the human evaluation, we chose the top-3 best- 266 performing LLMs across multiple settings. We 267 evaluated a total of 320 model-generated nuggets 268 with 37 ground-truth nuggets for three diverse ques- 269 tions across three different settings: Q0, QA1, and 270 QGDall. We evaluate the quality of each nugget 271 on the following criteria: (a) Correctness: whether 272 the generated nugget is correct (2), partially correct 273 (1), and incorrect (0); (b) Completeness: whether 274 the generated nugget is misleading (-1), not re- 275 quired (0), Okay, but not required (1), and re- 276 quired (2); (c) Precision: portions of the gener- 277 ated nuggets that are correct; (d) Recall: portions 278 of the ground-truth nuggets covered in the gen- 279 erated nuggets. We computed all the aforemen- 280 tioned scores for each question and averaged them 281 to report (Fig. 1) the overall scores. The human 282 evaluation of completeness and correctness criteria 283 reveals that under the ground-truth answers (QA1 284 strategy) all three LLMs’ performance was better, 285 only the question (Q0) strategy obtained the sub- 286 optimal performance. The evaluation also high- 287 lights that automatic precision and recall are highly 288 aligned with manual precision and recall. 289 4 Conclusions 290 This work presented a comprehensive study on 291 generating nuggets for health-related questions us- 292 ing various open and closed-source LLMs. Firstly, 293 we manually formulated nuggets for BioGen 2024 294 topics and thereafter, we devised multiple nugget 295 generation strategies to assess the capability of 296 LLMs under different settings. We found that most 297 LLMs obtained sub-optimal performance on the 298 task which demonstrates the challenge involved 299 with nugget generation, and we believe that our 300 manual-created nuggets will promote further re- 301 search in this direction. 302 4 Ethics Statement 303 The health-related questions and reference answers 304 used in this study are publicly available within the 305 Text REtrieval Conference (TREC) 2024 data. 306 Limitations 307 While the BioGen 2024 dataset covers a broad 308 range of question topics and intents sourced out 309 of popular health-related searches, it is not exhaus- 310 tive. Subsequently, our findings on the LLMs’ abil- 311 ity to generate nuggets in zero-shot settings apply 312 to information needs covered in the data: clinical 313 decision-support, factoid, and treatment and envi- 314 ronment effects. The manual nugget evaluation 315 approach outlined above can be used in the future 316 to expand the data. 317 Another limitation of the data is a single refer- 318 ence answer. While the bulk of the nuggets must be 319 present in any answer, some of the automatically 320 generated nuggets could have been present in alter- 321 native answers. For example, if the existing refer- 322 ence answer list surgery as a treatment option, with- 323 out specifying the best procedures, automatically 324 generated nuggets that name specific surgeries will 325 not get any credits for these nuggets. While this 326 may somewhat lower the scores, it should not affect 327 the model ranking, as the same approach is used for 328 all models. In the future, more than one reference 329 answer would be desirable to base the evaluation 330 on a nugget pyramid (Marton and Radul, 2006). 331 References 332 Marah Abdin, Jyoti Aneja, Harkirat Behl, Sébastien 333 Bubeck, Ronen Eldan, Suriya Gunasekar, Michael 334 Harrison, Russell J.
